II Was a very flustered and trembling little " General," who at last went up, armed with a table cloth, mid knocked at Horace Nicholl'e door. He was reading when she entered, and she mull not make up her mind to interrupt him. She spread the cloth with an elaborate care she had never, before bestowed on anything, and fidgethd about as long as ever she could, and still the words on her lips had to remain unspoken. At last just as she was turning to leave, Horace put down his book and spoke to give her some trifling order.

" Yes, sir," she answered breathlessly, and then, her grimy littlo face growing rosy with bluslieS, she launched into a torrent of confused thanks and apologies. Horace, who had not noticed the omission of words, so plainly had her eyes spoken her gratitude, was touched with pity and amusement. _ _

" I am very glad you like them," he said kindly. " But, look beiv, Rosina," he added a moment, "I wish you would not read such stuff as that you showed me." He looked at her and spoke in a gently serious way that filled her whole heart with worship and admiration. "It is not fit for a good little woman Rke you. You take my advice now, and read something better. There is so much good stuff," be went on, half to himself, forgetting that the child was still listen- ing, and hanging on his every word, "such tons of good stuff written, and yet these poor souls have their minds filled with such garbage as that, worse luck."

Rosina, vaguely realising that he was no longer addressing her, prepared to leave. "Pro- mise me not to read that paper any more," he said in a dangerously kindly tone, "and I will get you others. Are you fond of reading ?" " Yes, sir, thank you, sir," answered Rosina, all regrets for her lost paper vanishing, " but I won't read the' Plice Herald ' no more, sir." "That's a good girl," he answered lightly-. " What sort of stories do you like best ?" " Well, sir, I must say lam dearly fond of a novelette," she answered with a gravity which made him smile in spite of hiroself. "Novelettes," he said when she had gone. "How hard it is to understand the tastes of these people. I wonder when a love of poetry will be reached !"

When Horace returned to Plymouth Place after Christmas he brought back a collection of papers. During his holiday he had, to the wonderment of his friends, devoted much of his money and time to the purchase and perusal of novelettes and other inexpensive literature. "I want to become acquainted with the literature of the masses," he explained, " and I have come to the conclusion that their taste is a deal more decent than that of their so-called betters. A lot of these things are badly written, melodramatic and trashy, but others are pure, and grammatical, and all are perfectly decent." The first time be saw Rosina he asked her if she bad read the book he gave her. She blushed and hesitated, then stammered out that she had begun it. Horace was growing enlightened. " Don't you care for it ?" he asked kindly. " Oh, I daresay I shall when I gets into it more," answered [Wallin hurriedly, " it looks very nice further on. I have read a few lines in and out."
"I must begin lower down the intellectual scale," thought Horst* ruefully. "I wonder if you would like one of these," he asked, holding out one of the novelettes. Rosinats, face bright- ened.

"Oh, yes, sir, I had a piece of one Me this once and 't was beautiful. Yes, sir, please, sir; I think I should like this better than the other, it begins right at the beginning you see, oh, these are beautiful stories."

For some time after this Regina was kept on a course of novelettes. From the eagertess , with Which she devoured them Horace hoped that satiety would soon set in, and in this his hopes were fulfilled. One day she informed him, —she was quite friendly and confi- dential with him by that time,—that she had read her Christmas number. " And it is lovely," she cried enthusiastically, " I like it better than the novelettes. I've got a bit tired of them, they are so much alike." Long ere this there had been a marked change. in her appearance, her dull, shabby-looking hair was shining, and arranged not at all untastefully, her dress was neat, and there WAS a general air of trimness about her cap and apron. The next marked stage in her development was the finding by Horace of a piece of paper be- tween the pages of a book she returned to him, ca which was written a verso copied from the pages of the book itself: It was a simple, homely little poem, but very much to Resina'a taste, lir when he returned the paper to her she asked if there were any more verses, and was delighted when he lent her the whola'of the poem. " I am going to learn it by heart," she said. "You might be doing much better for yourself than you can do here. You should try to o'er. into a better class of place than this," said 'Horace one day. He forgot the poor harrassed landlady in his schemes for the redemption of Rositat. Regina looked distressed. " I know I might,' she said, " but I'm—l—l like it. here, mind I haven't got no one but myself to please., don't want to go away." Then she hurried out 'of the room. As she turned llorace thought he saw tears on her long lashes, but it might have been only afternlylis this,ir gi utitioii. Soon Horace Nicholls yea away for a holiday. He retained in such boisterously high ppirits that everyone was astimisheil. " Well, Rosie," he said, when she took him up his tea, " how are you. flow you've grown, and how nice you're looking. I have such n piece of news for you, Rosie. What do you think rye done since I have been away F"

He looked at a photograph he was holding in his hand, and up again st Silo was standing looking at him smilingly, ft puzzled look in her great brown eycs. " I can't tell, sir, I'm sure," she began, and then the smile stiffened on her lips, and her beat t soul. " I have got engaged, Rosa', engagecl to be married to Such a pretty young lady. ou should see her, Rosie, she'd to Ir ,I_, you open your eyes, 1 hO andpe she eMe day wiis yin will. ty interested, if 31.1;,0nn t„.(3: liii improving so, perhaps ewe day voti'll be ruble to come to live with us. ' fir iris exallation lie he• came effusive. Rositia laid her hand on the back of the nearest chair, and appeared to be trying to steady herself by it. " I am very—" she said slowly and painfully.., " I—l hope you nil be happy, sir." Then she turned away and looking at fthe door, wondered how she should reach it, it seemed so very far off, across an open space where there was nothing to bold by. But he was looking at her curiously, the thought braced her up. " Wouldn't. you like to see her photograph ?" Herm called nfter her. She stumbled hurriedly on, " Presently—please, sir. I must go for—for the rest of the things." Then she stumbled her way downstairs. Horace waited some time for her, then be sat down and began his tea. He wondered what it was she had gone for. 'and why she was so long, but other things soon claimed his thoughts. Rosina was below broiling chops in a blind, dazed way, with every vestige of colour faded from her face, and her breath coming in little moans, which even the fizzling of the chops did not drown.__

Horace did not see much of her in the days that followed, and when he did see her they did not talk as much as of old. She was always busy, and did not invite conversation, and he had lost interest in his schemes for her redemption, he had so much to think of too, be did not notice the change that had come over his pupil. He went away again before very long, to stay near nis nancee, Out wnen lie returnea true um% his cheerfulness was less pronounced. Rosins noticed it at once, and forgot her own pain in pity for his. She ceased to avoid him as she had done, and was untiring in her efforts to rouse and cheer him. But her numberless little cares and attentions were apparently lost on him, and his gloom remained unlightened. At last there came a day when, on going to re- move his breakfast things, she found him with his head bowed on his arms, an open letter in his hand. A little moan which escaped him from time to time, she had mistaken for his usual " come in." Ashamed of baying intruded she attempted to escape unnoticed, but Horace, realising- that he was not tilone, raised his head with is start and looked at her. The tears came rushing to her eyes at the sight of his sad ones. and his pa in .druwii face. Oh, is it you, Rosie, come in." Then his " head sunk into hisbiands again. " Are you in trouble, sir? Can I do anyibing for you I" she 11 sic ol gently, her mind, far from grasping the real state of a ffaim Sudden now, or dean, and a hurried • packing and de- parture were all that occurred lo her. " No, no," he groaned. kosina went on with iter work. Presently Horace rose and made an effort to pull himself together. "No one can help me, Rosie, thank yott," ho said. " will tell von what is wrong, you know k bout her, and I know I can trust you."_

Oh, yes,, sir, tend ll.OR,ina 'emphatically. " I never repeats nothing to nobody." You are a good little :,!oul, I know," said Horace, already t?ttched by the hooemt pathv exuresbed in every floe of her faue.

e went on, "it isn't much that •Is wrong after all, nothing uncommon, I suppose, only I—l, like a fool, trusted her." His face and voice grew hard and cynical; he found it was the easiest way to get the better of all other feelings. "My—the—the lady who was engaged to me has—bas seen someone she—likes better, and kai thrown me over. That is all."

Boothia stood transfixed. Pity for him, and an. other feeling she would not and could not define, were almost swallowed up in amazement that any girl could treat him AO. " Oh" she gasped at last, " bow could she." Horace gave a sharp laugh, unpleasant to bear, opened his mouth to speak, but remained silent. He told himself the old, old story, that for the future he would trust no woman, and so put himself beyond the risk of being deceived. Then his mood changed, and be, yearned for sympathy, yearned for the gentle consolation of a woman's voice.

" But here are no women left," he said to himself bitterly. "No wouienly, women. The creature that is grown now is simply a kind of sport and God only knows Auto what they will develop." Then his eyes fell on to a bunch of violets Rosina had brought him that morning. The scent and the sight of them reminded him of her. " Poor little Rosie, it is a shame to class them all together. She, at any rate, •is faithful and womanly too. One should train one's wife as I have trained Rosina, she should be of the- lower classes, with none of the false instincts, and here- ditary taints of their so-called superiors '." For the next few days lie was fully occupied in thinking. out a lot of nonsense, which to him was wisdom of the subtlest type, and the end of it all was that he asked Rosina to be his wife,—con- vinced that he was doing a good and noble action thereby. Rosina flushed crimson over face and neck when the great offer was made to her, and tears -of mortification bame into her eyes. She could not but think that " Mr. Horace, as she called him now, was having a joke at her expense. In her pain and resentment she told him so. " Laughing, Rosie I No, I am very far from laughter, unless you will be my wife. My dear, lam making you a serious and honourable offer, and one which I hope you will accept."

His seriousness cicilld her. This was so difier- ent to the love making which generally preceded and accompanied the proposal she had read of. If she had only dared she would have flung her arms about his neck and promised to love him for all time. To the lover of her imagination this would have been bliss indeed, but, somehow, she doubt- ed if Horace would be gratified with such a de- monstration. His new demeanour awed her. The prospect of being his wife frightened her. " I am not fit," she stanunered, " indeed, sir. I am not good enough for you. You would be —ashamed of me and I couldn't bear that. Please, sir, I would rather go on being your ser- vant." Tears stood in her eyes, and she was trembling visibly. • 'You are quite good enough for me," he said, you are the best and truest woman I ever met, and I should not have asked you to marry if I was ever likely to be ashamed of you." He spoke with all the lofty assurance of the ignorant. " You must leave here," he went on, growing a little more genial and natural in his manlier, as he began to plan their future. " Yon shall go to live with a lady for a year or two, and she will teach you all sorts of things you will need to know." Rosimis hear sank lower and •lower as this blissful prospeet was opened out before her. 4! Sit down," said Horace peremptorily, "Mrs. Mundy is out and will not want you yet." Rosinii, unaccustomed to sitting when in the Presence of the lodgers, perched • herself on the extreme edge Of the most uncomfortable chair in the room. Mr face was very white, and she was too embarrassed to raise bar eyes, When, at h•ligth, she left She room • e was not at all sure, whether she was engage sh d or not. _She could mot remember having any say in the matter, but elle supposed olio was, for Mr. Nicholls had talked so touch of what she was to do to • improve herself. ‘• He isn't pleased with me now, as I a,,,,'' she t hough t .w istfully..

Sho had to give a. month's notice to Mrs. Mundy, and nothing Horace said could induce iier to leave before tho time was up. Jo km lone- Mies. and fear of the future before her, site clung ,o her old mistre,s tenaciously. This month was ,0 her n respite before the dreaded polishing up ,rul improving process that Horace talked no mach of should begin. H(..race's holidays began a fortnight berOre WIIS to leave Mrs. Mandy, but he was to feet her the day site left, atid escort her at once to her new home. Perhaps his si.s.elice Wee IL good thing for the girl. Site min•seil him greatly, and appreciated. him the inure, loving lihn with her old love, divested of the nervous dread ,wlßch bad lately ovrrshado wed it ; lie had been very kind stud gentle when he had said good-bye, and had kissed her for the first time. "It seems wrong though, oven now, to be kissing the maid- servant," lie had said laughing, " doesn't it, ltosie ! But we will soon alter rill that, little WOllllOl. Front the moment you leave this house you must forget you ' have ever been a marvant, hot you lamt never change that lender little heart of yours.'' 'rho treatment she received from the other lodgers stood out in marked and disagreeable contrast, she resented now being called " slave)," and their coarse familiarity jarred on bar. She realised more than any nun how much her lover bad raised her front what alto was. -

Aweek went by, end no letter came from him. She was diseppointed but not surprised. She had never thrown elf the sense of her owu inferiority, and did not expect much attention from him. But she did think sometimes that the lovers she read of must be very unlike lovers in real life. They seemed-Im* she always pulled herself up when she foite4 h .rself wishing that Horace were more like a lova lii a book. She was very much surprised though, when, three days before the was to, leave, a cab dashed lip to the door and Horace himself stepped out, end ilurricd into the house. He was excited and seemed in high spirits, but, RO9lllll thought, rather strange and changed in his manner. He did not attempt to kiss her, when he met her, and he reemed to have a greet deal to say to 11rs. Mundy. So much that Rosina at last felt herself an intruder, and went away to prepare the dinner. It seemed plain to her that he kept Mrs. Mundy in conversatiou purposely to avoid being left Alone with her. Her mind as full of perplexity and indignation at such treatment. She was hurt cruelly end an angry gleam shone in her eyes: It was his duty to speak to her, to tell her the mean- ing of his sudden appearance,—at any rate not to treat her with less recognition than if she were • a dog. She vowed to herself she would not go near him again. But she had to take him his tea, and she went. But before she entered his room. she set her features in an expression of calm, proud indifference. It was no easy task, with her limbs trembling as they were, and her heart beat- ing so tumultuously that she thought he must see and hear it. But Horace was not far sighted enough to observe more than the expression of her face, and-that to him was reassuring just then. " Rosina," he said coughing a little to bide his embarrassment, while manfully trying to pluck up his courage or what was to come. " I have . something to say to you, I have a confession to make, and your forgiveness to ask." She looked up at him with alarm in her eyes. "You haven't done anything wrong," she asked incredulously. "No, no, nothing wrong at least," correcting himself, "nothing wicked—l mean —I must ex- plain to you, ilosina, I—think you will not blame me." He looked at her appealingly, but she stood immoveable, her face absolutely expression- less. A dim foreboding of what was coming was in her mind. Shb had gauged her lover better than either he or she was aware.

"While I was away," be went on, seeing that no help was to be had from her, " I—l met Amy again, and—oh it was all a mistake, Rosina. She never cared for the other fellow, she loved me all the time, and she nearly broke her heart about it. She broke off her engagement with him in less than a month, and—and ever since, oh she has fretted so, poor child, and when she saw me she could not—l must, in justice to you, Rosina, tell her secret, but I know I can trust you. She thought I had beard and had come, and I---I could not tell her about —about—" " Me," interposed Rosina harshly, unable to endure his flounderings any longer. He heaved a sigh of relief, " Yes, and—and.,.... she consldered—well—we thought it would be better for you—you woauld never be happy with me—and—and—well—we renewed, I—l said I would come and explain to you." Rosina's stillness and silence on receipt of this speech alarmed him more than any outburst would have done, it was not what he had prepared him-. pelf for, but her usually eloquent eyes were lowered, for she could not trust them, she knew they were more eloquent than her tongue. " Rosina," he burst forth, with all a man's im- patience at having to appear at a disadvantage, " Rosina, say something, say you forgive me, and think well of me. Oh, Rosina, shewe love each other so."
" As I loved you," Rosins said vain in the same harsh tone, but she spoke in the past, she Lad to pay that much deference to her self-re.

- - " Oh, how can I undo all-the mischief I have i done! Will you .free me Rosins, lam not good enough for you —" Rosina gave a little cynical laugh which was I more than half a sob, at any rate he was becom- ing like the lovers in the novelettes now, and the platitude died on his lips, it was too obvious. " Tell me," he went on ; he felt he must say something, that ghastly silence was unbearable. He had honesty enough in his soul to admit that Ile had acted badly, that he had never loved the girl, that he had sacrificed her solely and selfish- -19 tø his pride. " Would you like to leave here, 'Rosina P Will you—oh, what can I do .for you, dear—to make amends P" •

The endearment was too much for her, she raised her eyes and looked at him,, and he felt as though he had struck her. "Would to God you had done nothing," she cried bitterly. " Oh, why couldn't you have let me be." Her voice was thrilling with the exquisite pain she was suffering. ' "Why couldn't you have let me be, I was happy and content with my drudgery, InV ' Police Herald,' my life—l was happy for I knew nothing better, nor wanted it, but what 'can it be now. I hate it—and 'you have broken my heart—for a fancy—why couldn't you have Jet me alone? why couldn't you have let me alone ?" She sank down on a chair, and her head fell forward on her outstretched arms, as she had found him once, on that very spot. He went .close to her und laid his hand tenderly on her shaking shoulders, trying vainly to think of words which would not sound hollow or common- place, but before they came she had shaken his hand off fiercely. " Go—go away," she cried, " oh, for pity's sake go,—and leave me to face it out by Myself." The last words died away in a wail that brought tears to his eyes, and with that wail echoing in his ears he crept downstairs to the front door. "Rosina, Ros Ma." He heard Mrs. lkinndy's voice calling impatiently up the stairs. "What. ever are you dawdling so long about, and Mr. Simmons waiting for his tea, and his fish to cook and all, anyone would think—" He slunk out and closed the door softly behind him. He must get outside and walk quickly, the recollection of the way Rosina had taken it was more than he could endure. He wished she had not felt it—like that, it made him feel such a confounded brute,—and— He had a good mind to catch the next train back to Amy.; it might be kinder to Rosina, and it certainly would be pleasanter to him,— after all, he could do no- thing more, and m would get over it—in -time.

THE PALLOURAPH.

Dr. Otto Schick. of Hamburg, and Maihak, an instrument maker of that city, have brought out a "Pallograph" for re.;istering the vibrations of steamships, both vertipal and horizontal. The apparatus by analysing fhese vitirations is important for marine engineers and naval architects.
TRANSMITTING COMPASS INDICATIONS.

Messrs. Siemens and ilalskc, Irlin, at an exhi- bition of the German S ociety of Electricians sheaved an apparatus for transmitting the indications of a magnetic compass to a distance. Light is caused to vary the resistance of electric circuits between the transmitting compass and a second receiving compass in another place, so that the needles of one and the other are sympathetic, so to speak, and move concurrently.

div.head: TROPICAL DISEASE.
div.p: A TROPICAL DISEASE.

"Surra" is the name givA to a certain disease of the horse, cancel, ox, buffalo, and dog of India, Burmah, Indo-China, Dutch East India, the Philip- pines, and Mauritiu4,. caused by trypano- zomes. It appears from researches of MM. Leveran and 3lesnil that the Surra of Mauritius is of the same species as that. of India. There are, so far as the Globe knows, three varieties of Surra of a virulence decreasing in the following order: (1) the Surra of India; (2) that of.llauritius; (3) that of Mbori.

div.p: [ALL .KICIIITS ICEBERTILD.I
TIIE •REDENPTION OF ItOSINA,
M.. QUM-LER-COUCH (xluthor of" Jane Fereoe," ite.)

Already .that morning Rosina had been up and down the 'fifty stairs the house possessed, at least a dozen times. The last time she had staggered when she reached the top, mid had almost fallen over the can she was carrying, splashing the water over Gm stair-earpets, and bringing out Mrs. Mundy from the lop back room with a hastiness of step and speech that Rosina knew but never grow callous to. The next 1110. ment Rosina almost flew down the stairs mid up again with a cloth to wipe up the slop she had de. As soon as she had reitehed the top land- ing, a bell rang, and down she had to go again to the kitchen regions to see whew() bell it was. It belonged to, the young • gentleman on the second floor, be was going away; and wanted Bosnia to bolo him with his packing. The house, Number 17, Plymouth Place, was a lodging house, äutl Ilosina was, /14 Ahe proudly called herself, " the General." • Mrs. Mundy called her " my maid,". or more often she spoke of her in the plural, —perhaps because she did as nnieli work as two ordinary servants. Rosina felt only pride at being thus referred to, and no one thought of the unfairness of it to herself or the lodgers. The latter were well-meaning enough venlig men. who would have done 'natty things for themselves, and have saved Rosina's poor aching legs ninny a weary trot if they had known her as the little drudg-e she really was, (Miming mity ft a slave in that she was born white, nod bad laid a School Board education.

, . How long Ro,ista might have gone on being " they," nobody knows, if 14110 herself had not 'blown upon the mystery. It happened the very day she fell over the can of water. " young gentleman " who' was going away required a great deal of help with his packing, and Rosina was kept trotting up and dowsi to him with boots, 'supers, boxes, and other trifles. Luckily ho lived on the second floor, so Nosina could run up stud down two or three times without having to sit on a stair to rest and recover her breath.

ADA 119 she was going down for the last time, withii hat box in one band, and a bundle of rugs in the other, he called her back. " Here, Rosina, is something, to get yourself a Christmas present with." She dropped her load and went back. " There is half-a-crown for you, and one for the cook," lie said, holding out two half- crowns to ,ber.
Idositia'r; eager grimy liana fell slowly to her side. " Please, sir, there isn't no cook. I'm the General."

Horace Nicholls stared at her uncomprehend- ingly. " The what ?" lie asked. "The general, please, sir. Mts. Mundy only keeps one." " Oh—h, I see. You are maid-of-all-work, but—" he stopped. He was too good-hearted a fellow to expose the little conceits of his land- lady, but be felt staggered as he realised, though dimly it is true, the work the poor soul fend that wretched child bed to get through day after day. He felt remorseful when he remembered the num- ber of times, even, that very day, he had dragged that tired little mortal up stairs to wait on billi— on him, a strong man. ' Rosina, troubled by his silence, turned away to pick up his luggage again. She did not feel dis- appointed, for she had not had time to realise the fortune that had nearly been hers. She was only conscious of a first faint doubt as to the exalted position of a " general." But before she reached the door he came out of his reverie and stopped her.

"Here," he said, " take this," holding out the money. "If you have no fellow-servants, so much the hotter for you, for once. Buy yourself something for Christmas. Don't trouble to come up again," he added kindly. "I will not finish my packing until after lunch, and I need not bother you any more."

After Rosina as gone Horace sat pondering many things. He, was a good-natured, kindly fellow, with a strong strain of the philanthro- pist in his composition, and, while sitting there hugging his knee, he realised that here was a chance at his hand, to work out a long-cherished idea. Here was a life into which he might bring some beauty, something ennobling, he could fill her soul with lofty ideals, and teach her to under- stand the beauty of life. He grew quite fired with his project. . . . . . .

After -Zurich he went out and walked about looking at the shops, hoping to gather hints for the first step. A picture shop caught his eye, and he gazed thoughtfully at prettily framed photo- graphs of great soul-inapinng pictures. Then came a- bookshop, its windows fan of treasures that filled his soul with longings. He won- dered, rather gloomily, how long it would take to teach such a creature aiS Boehm to appreciate these things. He returned home with a box of sweets, and the Christmas number of a very re- spectable but not too highly cultured magazine. By the time he got back to Plymouth Pine° the lamps were lighted. It was tea time, and he had not fihished his ruching yet. Luckily he was not leaving until the night train. When he got in, he carried his parcels up to his room and looked through the magazine to see if it was quite :suit- able for a girl of abont sixteen or seventeen. Then lie began to wonder how he should give them to her. [To went over to his bell to ring for her, but recollecting how mauy times he lied rung her up that day already, hesitated. At. last he determined to go down awl look for her in her own domain. The determination was prompt- ed partly by kindness, partly by curiosity. He groped his way down the steep, dark kit- chen stairs,—lie knew that Mrs. Mundy was safely out,---wondering all the time Low the child ever managed to get up and down them alive with the heavy trays and loads she had to carry. The grimy aspect of the place depressed him. A faint light, shining through an open doorway. only auentuated the gloom ; hut it, and the mind of a chair being pushed back hurriedly, guided him to the kitchen. Rosina had been at her lea, at least at the meal courteously called by that name. There was no cloth on the table, a large cup stood before her containing an unwholesome looking decoction which was neither tea nor pure water, and was innocent of milk or sugar, while in the saucer which she was using as a plate, lay a partly eaten slice of bread with some dripping craped over it. Her look of amazement roused Horace to a sense of the unfitness of his proceed- sing. Ile hastily put the sweets and the book down before her.

"I have brought you some sweets, and some- thing to read," he said, half shyly. "I know girls are fond of sweet things, and I think you will like these stories. They will amuse you, per- haps," he finished lamely, saying nothing of what was in his mind to say, but filled with won- der as to how with those startled, uncompre- hending eyes fixed on him he could ever hope to teach the child the beauty of anything. " Are you fond of reading ?" be asked. Then he saw that in the hand which hung by her side she held a paper. -
" Yes sirr,"' she answered, shyly. " What is that you have there?" _ .

She produced -the paper, " 'Tis the Police Herald, " she answered, end then, waxing holder, as she noted his interest, "it has got lots of pictures in it, there's one there of the woman that murdered her children last week, and one of 'er cutting 'er own—" With an exclamation •of disgust Horace snatched the paper front her. "What an abomin- able thing," he cried wrathfully, " they ought to be had up for publishing such stuff. It is dis- gusting, revolting, but—" catching sight of Ro- sine's face he controlled himself. It is bad for ' anyone to see such papers," he said more gently. Then he thanked Rosins for her attention to him, and wishing her a happy Christmas left her and made his way back to his own room. When he reached it he found that he had brought awly Rosins.'s paper with him, and he felt really pleased that it was out of her hands. " I am afraid my Christmas number will be but tame after this, he said, glancing through the sheet, with an invective for everything his eyes fell on. Itosina below stairs, bemoaned her lost paper bitterly, also she felt sorry that Mr. Nicholls had disapproved of it, she wished that she lied not shown it to him. Then she turned with delight to her presents. It was some time before she could make up her mind to untie the silken ribbon about the box, and when at last she did, she had not the heart to break the rows of pretty choco- lates. She had never seen anything like them be- fore. So she closed the box without tasting the •contents, and opened her book. It was well illus- trated, and full of good stories, the pictures in- terested her much, and she read a few lines here and there, but she soon laid it aside and took up her sweets again. " I won't begin it yet," she said. half apolo- getically. " I can't settle to nothing. What a kind gentleman Mr. Nicholls is—and I never thanked him, proper. No, I don't believe I so much as said thank you.' "

div.head: DESERTED WIFE'S CLAIM FOR COMPENSATION.
div.p: DESERTED WIFE'S CLAIM FOR COMPENSATION.
Judgment for the Respondents.

His Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands gave his decision in the Birkenhead County Court on Tuesday, in regard to the claim made by Ann Dawson, Stockport, against Messrs. Joseph Crosfleld and Sons, Limited, for com- pensation for the death of her husband. The claim was originally heard at the Warrington County Court when Mr. F. Cuthbert Smith (instructed by Mr. T. S. Steel) appeared for the applicant. Mr. Rigby Swift instructed by Messrs. Richardson and Marsh, appearing for the respondents. It will be remembered that Dawson was killed at the respondents works when attending an elevated settling tank. Some years previous to his death he deserted his wife and during the period covered by the desertion had not contributed to her maintenance. Respondents' contention was that Mrs. Dawson was not depenlent upon her husband at the time of his death and was therefore not entitled to compensation. After hearing the arguments of the respective counsel his Honour reserved judgment, which he delivered on Tuesday to the parties concerned. His Honour found that the applicant was neither wholly or partially dependent at the time of the man's death, and he there- fore decided in favour of the respondents with costs on Scale B," which were not to bs enforced unless the applicant served notice of appeal.

I"HISTORIC SITES AND SCENES OF ENGLAND,"—rs the title of a sumptuously got-up work published by the Greet Western Railway Company. Ostensibly the volume has been prepared for American travellers, as an introduction and guide to the varied beauties of English scenery, and the vast wealth of England's historical associations. But while it very eloquently , fulfils this aim, the volume also tells many of us homesters a deal that we should know of our own holiday possibilities. There is, also, much real literary merit about the publication, which is profusely end elaborately illustrated, and in every essential is "a guide, philosopher, and friend." But it is not a guide of the advertisement order.

div.head: WOMAN'S REALM.
div.p: WOMAN'S REALM.
DRESS-FASHION-HOME;
FEMALE SWINDLERS AT HOTELS.

Some of the most dangerous female swindlers in the world are to be found in fashionable hotels, writes Mr. Geo. R. Sims. They fre- quentl7 have foreign titles. Princesses, marchionesses, countesses, and baronesses there are. who are well known to the international police,. and who yet continue to live luxuriously year in, year out, on a methodical system of fraud. Few of them are young—many of them are middle-aged, and some are elderly. But they rarely fail to pay their expenses, though they may fail to pay the tradespeople they honour with their patronage. Even in this matter, how- ever, they are careful, and avoid, if they possibly can, any transaction with a shopkeeper which might lead to the publicity of the police-court. A charge of swindling would be inconvenient. It would necessitate the adoption of a new title, and that would be awkward, because the majority of these adventhresses are too well known to certain people in fashionable resorts to be able to change a title without exciting suspicion.

div.head: VOILE DRESS.
div.p: A VOILE DRESS.

In spite of the many new materials offered foi our choice this season, voile still remains u popular as it has ever been. The dress shewn in our sketch is made of champagne-coloured voile. The blouse-shaped bodice has a deep round collar, crossed in front, and is edged by s band of pierced embroidery worked on ivory

silk. This embroidery reappears on the little vest disclosed in the opening of the bodice. Full puffs form the sleeves, which terminate at the elbow in frills of lace, patterned to match the- embroidery on the collar. The akirt is quite- plain, and is gathered at the waist, falling in soft folds to the feet. A deep belt of Pompa- dour silk, in delicate shades of pink,' mauve, and green, adds a touch of oolour to the costume.

GOSSIP. Daring a lecture delivered at Oxford by Miss Edith Pitcairn, photographs thrown on the screen shewed the lecturer in her garden at Haslemere, with birds perched on her fingers. She knows all the birds in her garden so well that they answer her call when she utters their pet names.

Marriage no longer being the aim of every girl's existence, she can be far more safely trusted, says the World, to make friends witk the other sex, and form her own opinions on love, than her predecessors who saw possible husbands in all the men they met.

In a matrimonial suit heard at Brooklyn a wife sought separation on the ground that:her husband had been spending all his income in an attempt to solve the problem of perpetual motion. certainly we women seem to work better its leagues, judging from their quite bewildering increase. A new regimes of activity is assured to the "Girls' Guild--of Service-and Good Fellowship," now numbering 2,600 members, by the acceptance of the honorary /secretaryship by Miss Sinclair, sister of the Archdeacon of London. LITTLE GIRL'S DRESS. The summer ' will soon be upon us, and mothers are already thinking of dainty dresses for their children. Linen, lawn, and mercerised lawn are especially, suitable materials for the little dress shown in the sketch. The dress is gathered into a rather deep band, to which is attached loops of whito embroidered lawn. A soft-blue ribbon is passed through the loops, and

tied in a bow at the side. The hem of the short, fall skirt is finished with tucks, and edged with narrow Valenciennes lace. The round yoko iS outlined with embroidered lawn, narrow blue ribbon being threaded through. Tho opening at the neck is filled in with lawn, drawn up to a tiny frill round the throat. A berthe, composed of two frills edged with lace, gives, width to .the little figure. The sleeve:. arc gathered into bands above the elbow, and finished with ribbon, threaded through embroidered loops, and tied 111 small bows.
Wino' SHALL IT BE?

Shall we sit down under the slur that has been Cast upon our symmetry by a writer on coming modes? asks "Ambrosia" in the World. It has been decreed this season that we shall reveal by day as well as by night what Nature has done for us in the way of arms. Our sleeves have been literally rolled up for us by Madame La Mode. Across the Channel they are wearing the long gloves which this fashion entails quite tightly drawn up, while we are at great pains that ours shall be wrinkled and rucked. And for why? as our Hibernian friends say. It is, so our detractors aver, because our arms are ugly. Now, shall we accept this, or shall we demonstrate the falsehood oi the accusation by pulling our cloves taut and trig), and displaying the real shape of our arms? OUr symmetrical reputation is actually trembling in the balance.

div.head: MAGAZINE CUTTINGS.
div.p: MAGAZINE CUTTINGS.
MASSAGE.

Massage is the oldest form of surgical treatment known to man. It is practically the only form known to animals, whose instinct causes them to lick or rub any part which gives them pain. Rubbing down a man after battle was a custom of the ancient Greeks, just as it is our present practice to rub down a horse. Hippo- crates recdimmended rubbing for stiff joints, and it was a recognised treatment among the Greek doctars. But, in addition to its employment for remedial purposes, it was,and still is,used as a luxnry,being -part of the process now known as a Turkish bath.—Mr. J. Danvers Power, in the" Nursing Times." SMALL HOLDINGS. - - -

The history of small holdings in England is full of interest. The oldest of them were, no doubt, given by the knights and barons to favourite retainers, for services in the field and otherwise, though in the manorial system there could not have been any con- siderable number of small owners. A great many came into existence, however, in the time of Elizabeth, when, as now, it was found extremely difficult to keep people on the land, and the Government of the day had to devise special encouragements to induce them to do so. These small holdings endured well on into the nineteenth century, and in many parts'of the country the houses still remain, though the holdiags themselves have been merged in the large estates.—" Country Life." THE PARISIAN HOLIDAY-MAKING. Men and women at the tables d'hôte behave alike. They all wipe their glass, plate, and fork with their table napkin, and then tuck one corner of the said napkin into their collar. Then the business of the day begins. They eat fairly well, and only occasionally do you see someone serve himself to asparagus with his fingers, or put his knife in his mouth; the majority know better. But they all clean their plates with a piene of bread; they never leave a drop of gravy—it is too good to be wasted. And as in this class of hotel the knives and forks are not changed daring the courses, it is well to notice how the habitue manages to get the taste of the last dish off the blade and prongs. We may smile at this custom of one man one knife and Tork, but when we consider it calmly, why should we require fresh cutlery for the different dishes? From the point of view of cleanliness we are better off to keep our knives and forks than have them washed and returned in the so-called civilised fashion. I begin to think I would rather wipe my fork on a piece of bread than have it dipped in a bucket of greasy water and dried on the common cloth, as must occur oftener than we know. Frances Keyzer in" The King." COWS WITH SHOES.

• • • --- I n Peru cows must submit to a curious custom. There they are never allowed tu roam all day in the lush grass of meadows, but are kept on the roofs of their house; The big rsmbling houses of Lima have adobe roofs, flat as floor-boards, and there are hundreds of them in the suburbs of that proud old city which serve the purposes of a barnyard. Thither the calf is called, with pigs, goats, and fowls as her companions, and there she stays for the rest of her days. Horses and mules, by the way, are invariably housed In the lower room, for in Spanish America it is not the fashion for folk to inhabit the ground floors of their houses. In Switzerland and Buenos Ayres, too, cows must wear shoes. It is the custom in the nrgentine Republic, where the roads are extremely rough and hard, for the milkman to make his round, taking his cow with him, and 'drawing off the milk as required by each house- holder. The streets being paved with badly trimmed stones, the hoofs of a cow that were unshod would be badly cut by the sharp, projecting edges. In Switzerland it is considered that cows which are shod and kept in regular exercise, such as ploughing and carting, keep more healthy, and consequently give a better quality and greater quantity of milk.—" Smith's Weekly. '

" SWINDLER'S IN PRESS surrs. Mr. Geo. R. Sims, writing in "Pearson's Weekly " on the subjects of sharks who prey on the upper classes says There are plenty of people in London to-day whose legitimate income is under £l.OO a year, and who yet live in well-appointed houses in good neighbourhoods, keep servants, and entertain on a lavish scale. In the great London hotels there are always anurnoer of guests who are nothing but adventurers and adventuresses. The well-dressed, well-mannered "dangerous class" has increased rapidly of late years. The conditions of modern life are wholly favourable to its development. The breaking down of social barriers which has marked the new century has opened up new and profitable fields of enterprise. In a day when millionaires spring up like mushrooms and anybody with an American accent or a Jewish name is accepted as fabulously rich "without further inquiry," it is the easiest thing in the world for the skilful ad- venturer to work himself into any society—even to obtain the entr4o to houses where, once having been seen, his reputation is hall-marked. No one, as a rule—except a tradesman swindled out of his goods—seeks to pry into the mystery of these people's means. The source of the incomes of so many who live luxurionsly to-day is a mystery, thus suspicion has been lulled, and anyone with a few pounds and a portmanteau or a Saratoga trunk has only, to put up at a welt-frequented London liotel to start making a use- ful circle of acquaintances at once."

div.head: HOW THE PANAMA CANAL MAY BE DUG.
div.p: HOW THE PANAMA CANAL MAY BE DUG.

For those sections of the Panama Canal which lie in the coastal plains, as from Colon to Bohio on the Atlantic side and from Mirallores to Panama on the Pacific, hydraulic dredges may be used effectively to deal with all the soft material. In these sections of the work it is of the first importance that no manual labour should be necessary on shore, as the banks are covered with typical vegetationand it would be difficult, if not impossible, to handle large discharge-pipes on shore under such conditions. The first requisite for hydraulic dredging in those sections is to throw up a large embankment on either side to retain the material •deposited. Such an embankment may be made by a powerful clipper dredge, making its own ckannel and tasting on the bank. Such a dredge could cut through any obstructions in its way and not a man need step off the dredge. This operation done, we have two

div.head: bocot OF ME PENGUIN.
div.p: THE bocot OF ME PENGUIN.

The Penguins of Macquarie Island and, the desolate Micklands are in danger of extermination at the hands of the company promotor, and this fate will certainly overtake them unless steps are taken to save them. Dr. E. A. Wilson noints out that for some years past a con- siderable trade has gone on in the preparation of pen- guin oil, which is obtained by casting these unfortunate birds by the thousand into the melting-pot and boiling them down. No less than 100 tons of oil so procured has recently been placed on the market. Encouraged by success, a scheme is now afoot whereby cauldrons are to be set up on the Auckland Islands to facilitate this nefarious traffic. Hitherto the " rookeries " of these Islands have suffered comparatively little ; but once the cauldron fires are lighted they will not be allowed to die out till the last survivor of the host has been flung into the seething broth. Surely no effort should be spared to frustrate this diabolical scheme.— Knowledge."

div.head: FIRST ASSAULT ON PORT ARTHUR.
div.p: THE FIRST ASSAULT ON PORT ARTHUR.

! This grand assault—the first—began on August 19. For seven days and nights, withoutcessation, the battle raged, in the vain endeavour to pierce that right centre. It is said that the Japanese are all heroes—that none are cowards. Some are also sensible. There was the Eighth Regiment, which, when ordered into the assault, where the one before it had been swept down, sent back word, through its commanding officer, that the way was impossible. Ths word was so new to the brigee- general that he ordered the regiment to the rear for fatigue duty, the worst punishment that can come to a japanese soldier in an army where they have no guard- houses. Another regiment, the immortal Ninth, was ordered to cross the field to the foot of the slope on which lay, dead and dying, many of the men of the regiment which had gone before. The colonel, Takagagi, surveying what was to be accomplished, sent back word that it was not feasible. The brigade-general, Ichinobe, replied hotly that one regiment was enough to take one battery. Takagagi stepped out of the ravine, in which he had , been seeking shelter, at the head of his men. Before he bad been marching, as colonels usually do, in the rear, while his line officers led the advance. Now he leaped forward up,the slope, the first. A &oxen paces from the ravine he fell, with four bullets through his breast. The lieutenant-colonel took up the lead, and was shot a few yards further. The majors were wiped out. Every captain but one went down. The last captain, . Nashimoto, in charge of D Company, found himself, at ! length, under the Chinese Wall with seventeen men.— From "Port Arthur, its Siege and Fell," in the "Corn- hill Magazine " for May.

div.head: IT TOUCHED HIS HEART.
div.p: IT TOUCHED HIS HEART.

In one of Mr. E. Thompson Seton's thrilling stories of wild animal life, appearing in the" Windsor," he relates the following : "It was a very rainy summer, the woods were wet and soft everywhere, and the young hunter was led to follow tracks that would have defied an expert in drier times. One day he came on piglike footprints in the woods. He trailed them with little difficulty, for they were new and a heavy rain two hours before had wiped out all other trails. After following half a mile, they led him to a little, open ravine, and as he reached its brow he saw across it a flash of white; then his keen young eyes made out the forms of a deer and a spotted fawn gazing at him curiously. Though he was on the trail, they gave a start. He gazed at them open-mouthed. The I mother turned and raised the danger flag, her white tail, I and bounded lightly away, to be followed by the young- ster, clearing low logs with an effortless leap, or bend- ing down with catlike suppleness when they came to a log upraised so that they might pass below it. He never again got a chande to shoot at them, though more than once he saw the same two tracks' or believed they were the same, as for some cause never yet explained deer were scarcer in that unbroken forest than they were in later years when clearings spread around. once--

He never saw them ; but he saw the mother he thought it was the same—she was searching the woods with her nose, trying the ground for trails ; she was nervous and anxious, evidently seeking. He gently stooped, took up a broad blade of grass, laid it between the edges of his thumbs, then blowing through this simple squeaker, he made a short, shrill bleat, a fair Imitation of a faVvn's cry for the mother, and the deer, though a long way off, came bounding towards him. 1 He snatched his gun, meaning to kill her, but the movement caught her eye. She stopped. Her mane bristled a little; she sniffed and looked inquiringly at him. Her big, soft eyes touched his heart; held back his hand; she took a cautious step nearer, got a full whiff of her mortal enemy, bounded behind a big tree, 1 and away before his merciful impulse was gone. Poor I thing ! ' he said ! 'I belive she has loather little one." —For the rest of this story see the May" Windsor Magazine," a remarkable number, which includes a large instalment of Rider Haggard's thrilling sequel to" She"; another complete episode in the new romantic series by. Agnes and Egerton Castle ; and a long story of motor matters by Robert Barr, complete in the one number. The wealth of good articles include "The Commissariat of our Railways" and an appreciation of the art of Mr. Seymour Lucas, R.A., which is accompanied by no less than sixteen] beautilul reproductions of his finest , pictures.

" I am not anxious about you, Jermy," Jordison broke in abruptly, "what about the house ? "
"It stands," Jermy replied, "I've not been in it, and shan't till the smoke's gone. The engine house is now an 'ole in the ground, ati far as I can see."

! "Where's Susanson ? " ' i Iding n a ditch, and calling down tht wrath of 'eaven on yer 'ead." Jordison laughed. At any rate the (Red House was not in ruins. He had no further use for the engine-house. Then his voice grew stern..
"Who's been fooling with the dynamite ? " he said abruptly._ . _

"Better Susanson," the man replied. "He's been poking about in the shed all the morning." For three hours the men waited and watched the smoke 'Dour away towards the east. The air was full of smuts and their faces grew black with soot. From where they sat they could feel the fierce heat of the blazing petrol. Half a dozen times they worked their way round the foot of the hill, and tried to ascend the other side to the house. But the thick smoke drove them back, and they realised that they would have to wait until the fire had burnt itself out.

During this period of waiting they had several visitors. Men came up on carts and bicycles, some even in boats, all anxious to discover the cause of the great column of smoke that had been seen for miles round like the pillar of cloud that had guided the Israelites in the wilderness. But each and all were courteously sent about their business. Jordison explained the disaster in a few words, and expressed his capability to deal with it without any aid but that of his servants. Towards dark the blazing spirit burnt itself out. The flames dwindled down to flickering sheets of blue, sweeping along the ground and spouting up from crevices where the petrol still lay hid. The dense volume of smoke died away into a thick stream of vapour that the wind scattered as soon as it formed.

Susanson emerged from ,his hiding place and name crawling up with a request for food and water. He was 'questioned as to the ex- plosion, but nothing could be got out of him. Both Lipp and Jermy kicked him, and Jordi- &on did not interfere. Then all four men made then way to the Red House. In the fadit.g light they could see the ravages wrought by the explosion. The sngine-house was, as Jermy had said, a mere hole in the ground, a pit of smoking debris. From it, as from the centre of a star, ran great tracks and fissures in the rock, some nearly two feet in width.

The Red House itself still stood, but there was not a pane of glass in the windows, and not a chimney left standing on its roofs. The walls were seamed with narrow cracks, and the whole building leant two or three degrees lut of the peipendicular. On two sides it was as black as though it had been built of coal, but it had fortunately been beyond the reach of the flames, and ,only the smoke had teuched it.

Within they found a veritable chaos. Most If the ceilings had come down in a shower of plaster, and the bare laths showed through Like the bones of a skeleton. Pictures, orna- ments and crockery lay heaped on the floor, the Wall paper was covered with ominous lines, and every room that the oily smoke had penetrated was black with soot.

Jordison made a careful inspection of the walls and came to the conclusion that there was no immediate danger to the main struc- ture of the hou'§e. He sent off Jermy and Susanson to prepare a meal, for they had eaten nothing since breakfast, told Lipp to stop up the windows of the dining-room with canvas, or whatever else he could find, and then, lighting a lantern, made his way down into the cellars. He had yet to satisfy him- self about the foundations of the house. He descended the stone steps cautiously, holding the lantern above his head, and examining the walls on either side. One of the steps had been displaced and rocked as he placed his foot upon it. The cellar itself was cut out of the solid rock, faced with brick and paved with flag- stones. Jordison threw the light of the Lantern carefully round as he stood at the bottom of the steps. The floor was littered with broke% glass and swimming with wine. Jordison placed his hand in it and drew it out dripping and crimson. Six dozen bottles of claret had been, flung out from their bins and dashed to pieces. - - - .

He picked his way among the debris and carefully examined the floor and wills. There were two narrow fissures in the brick-work, and one deep crack across the stone flags. The force of the explosion must have been terrific. It seemed probable that the whole mass of rock on which the house stood had been cracked in every direction. Then suddenly, as Jordison stood on one ot the broken flag-stones, it tilted and split. The ground seemed to sink away under his feet, and there was the sound of falling rock beneath him. Quick as thought he flung himself back and clutched one of the wine bins an the wall. The woodwork lurched towards him and the bottles flew from their places. Underneath his feet the ground dropped away, and he could hear bottles and pieces of stone falling into some cavity beneath. He tried for a foothold, and the wine bin moved another degree outward. Then he hung still, and felt the whole structure lean further and further from the wall.

At last it ceased to give but trembled in the balance. Three yards to the .left the over- turned lantern lay on solid stone. He thanked God that it still gave light. He acted quickly. Hand oVer hand he moved along the wine bin. With every movement it quivered and seemed about to fall over into the depths below. But it held till his legs struck the edge of the hole. With a final effort he drew himself up on to the floor, and rolled over and over towards the light. As he did so, the wine bin came toppling over and far below he heard the crash of broken glass. He crawled to the foot of the steps and lay there panting for breath. • He did not under- stand what had happened, but it seemed to him as though the whole world were crumbling away beneath his feet. He knew that he must ascend the steps. Yet for the moment he could not stir, but lay inert, helpess 'motionless as a log. His clothes were soaked with wine, and the fumes of it rose to his brain.
Then with a violent effort he roused himself, sprang to his feet, and touching the walls on either side of him, as though afraid that they would elude his hands, staggered up the stairs.
That night they all slept in the loft over the 1, stables. Jordison told them plainly that the 1 house itself might fall through the crust of the earth at any moment, _ _ _

But the next morning Jordison told Lipp to get a rope knd a couple of lanterns. He was determined to investigate what lay beneath the cellar, and find out for himself whether it would be safe to remain any longer in the Red House.

Lipp made the rope fast to one of the bars of the pantry window at the head of the stairs, and taking the heavy coils on his arm, moved cautiously down to the cellar, and flung. them into the black gulf that yawned beneath thim. They could hear the rope 1 strike the bottom, and knew that it was long enough for their purpose. Then Jordison placed a rug between the rope and the jagged edge of the broken flagstones and, hanging the lantern round his neck, lowered himself hand over hand into the pit. When he had descended about twenty yprds his feet found foothold on the bottom, and he called out to Lipp, who proceeded to follow him. Jordison watched the spark of light descending like a star through the dark- ness, until tilt servant reached his side. The floor beneath them was strewn with debris, broken rock, and flooring, spattered with glass and drenched with wine. The bin lay two yards away from them, a crushed and splintered frame of woodwork. Jordison wedged one of the lanterns firmly between two pieces of rock and took the other from Lipp's hand. He picked his way care- fully through the fallen glass and stone till he reached a wide expanse of smooth floor, stretching as far as the light iwuld penetrate. He stooped down and examined it. Then he brushed away the 'layer of dust that covered sit. caul gave an excaamation of surprise. For

underneath this soft carpet spreaa by the hand of nature through many centuries, appeared, the regular squares of •a tesselated pavement, black and red alternately, highly* glazed and beautifully designed. In a moment he knew that he had made a dis- covery of great archmological interest. With out a doubt the place, whatever purpose it served, was the work of the Romans. A closer inspection revealed a large cham- ber nearly too feet square. The walls were smoothly chiselled from the solid rock, but here and there a deep rough hollow in the surface showed that the room was a natural cavity in the hill, and that the hand of man had merely planed and shaped it to its present regular form. In places the faint outlines of frescoes were visible on the walls, but time had redu d the paint to a dull blur of colour, an indistinct shadow of what had once been, perhaps, the work of a great artist. Jordison was less interested in archmology than in the safety of his house. And the most beautiful frescoes in the world would not have , distracted his attention from a crack in the rock that lay beneath it. By the feeble light of the lantern he scanned every inch of the surface within view. He discovered , two small fissures on opposite sides of the cham- ber. From the position of the light he had left burning at the foot of the rope he calcu- lated that the crack was continuous from one side of the room to the other, and that it ran through the hole in the cellar floor. It was evident that the rock had given way at its weakest point. On one side of this great chamber there was a large opening ten feet square, and on the other a smaller one, no bigger than an ordin- ary doorway. The two men explored the latter first, and found that it led into another room about zo feet by 16 feet, and rz feet high. This again led into another and yet another apartment. In all there were seven rooms of various sizes, each one of them a joy to the antiqUarian. The tesselated pavement in one of them surpassed in beauty anything of the sort that had ever been found in the British Isles. It was a dull purple, veined with gold, and the gold beneath its glaze was as bright as the day it had been laid on by some Roman craftsman. Traces of the vanished occupants were few and far between. Half a dozen pieces Of pottery, three brass coins with indecipherable inscriptions, a piece of steel that might once have been partj of the blade of a sword, thick piles of dust, sown with small nails, perhaps all that was left of luxuriant couches and richly carved tables. These, with one excep- tion, were all that the itasters of the world had left behind them.

This exception lay in the last room of all. A tiny chamber scarcely to feet \ square. Here, half hidden in a great. heap of dust, lay the bones of a man. The fleshless fingers of his right hand still touched a small bone cross. God only knows what tragedy of faith lay hidden hr this silent tomb.

Jordison and Lipp betrayed no interest in their discoveries, and retracing their steps, commenced to explore the larger opening on either side of the great hall. It proved to be a mere tunnel, sloping downwards into the earth. The roof and walls were rough and irregular, varying in height and width to such an extent that it was quite evident that the passage was the work of nature and not of man. The latter, however, had done good work on the floor. This had been smoothed down to a surface at least as good as a country* road. Neither Lipp nor Jordison noticed the remarkable difference between the floor and the walls. But an expert would have told them that the Romans were a military nation, and whereas they cared nothing for what lay above or on either side of them, they cared much for the surface that their soldiers had to march over.

The tunnel apparently led, to no further chambers, but ran on in a straight line toward the east. When the two men had trabersed it about half a mile, it ceased to slope down- wards. They walked on for an hour, and still did not come to the end of the passage. It began to curve and wind in various direc- tions. But Jordison consulted a small compass which hung on his watch chain, and found that the general trend of the passage was still towards the east. Lipp was for turning back, but jordison insisted on, going forward. His curiosity was aroused. He guessed that the tunnel did not lead aimlessly into the bowels of the earth. He fancied, too, that the air. was unusually /fresh, and opening the glass of the lantern, the flame flickered with the faint draught that moved towards them.

They walked on for another hour, Lipp cursing at every step they took, and even Jordison began to wonder whether they had better not retrace their steps. His opinion of the Romans neared a vanishing point. It seemed a lamentable waste of time and energy to construct a road of this sort.

At last they came to the end of the passage. It terminated, not in a blank and solid wall, but in a heaped-up pile of rock. The roof had fallen in and barred all further progress. It was impossible to tell whether the end was just beyond the barrier, or whether the tunnel still ran miles further into the west. As far as Lipp and Jordison were .concerned, this was the end. Yet Jordison still fancied that the air percolated through the heap of broken stone that la Y in front ot him, and the candle, burnt almost to the socket, flickered gently when he opened the front of the lantern.

There was nothing more to be done, and • certainly nothing rnpre to be seen. Jordison put a new candle in the lantern, and the two men retraced their steps. If was nearly dark when they emerged from the cellar and breathed the fresh air again. Neither Lipp nor Jordison attv,ched any importance to their day's work. The former characterised it as "a piece of tom- foolery." The latter could not make up his mind whether the house rested on a safe foundation or not. Certainly neithrei of them guessed that their future existence Would depend on the handiwork of men who had died before the dawn of civilisation in England.

Yet even then beneath the debris of plaster in the hall of the Red House lay a letter which the postman had slipped through the slit in the door the previous afternoon, and which was destined to direct William Jordison's career into a channel of which he had not as yet the faintest knowledge, and for which a., yet he had not the faintest desire. (To be continued.) j

div.head: By J. B. HARRIS BURLAND.
div.p: By J. B. HARRIS BURLAND.
CHAPTER X.
A BURIED'PALACt.

When Jordison had despatched the telegram. to Messrs. Briggs and Warlock, he tried tc thrust the matter from his mind, and threm aimself heart and soul into the construction oi his new motor car. Day after 'day he shut himself up in the little room that looked out over the eastern marshes, and night after night he sat at the deal table till his brain grew too weary to think; and the plans and figures swam before his eyes. . .

Happy is the mind that can forget its sorrows in work, or dull its pain in sheer weariness of physical exertion. Jordison worked hard and he worked late, but he could not forget that this work w4s far removed from the purpose of his life. Never an hour passed in which he did not turn away from the papers before him, and think of the son that was lost to him or of the woman with whom he had yet settle a long standing account. And even his wife had her place in these moments of remembrance. He could plainly see the bowed head on the desk, feel the stiffened arms, and read from the tear-stained page the poem he had marked for her in the days of their courtship. It was the curse of his life, that he could not forget. He fought with the memories, and beat them down into oblivion, and turned to his work with renewed energy. The pangs were short, for he stifled them, but they were insistent and inevitable. Two or three minutes, perhaps, out af .each hour, but every second of these minutes foil to the brim with pain. Yet for all these interruptions, Jordison's • mind worked with mechanical precision. It was the mind of an expert moving steadily in a fixed direction, neglecting no chance that might lead to ultimate success, weighing every possibility, working DU t every calculation with exactitude. The moments carat when all the work became a chaos, and figures and plans were whirled away like dust in a storm. But the rest of the time Jordison's mind was calm and even. Every line was lrawn true and firm, e*ry calculation was absolutely accurate, even to ten places in decimals.

And success came io Jordison at last, as it cornea to most men With an earnest purpose. The whole of one day and the whole of one night he sat at his deal table and made calculations, and measured lines and drew plans to scale. And when the grey light of morning came through the window it showed a white face still poring aver a growing heap of papers, a white haggard face with a gleam of triumph in the restless eyes. And on paper the motor car had become an accomplished fact.

Jordison was no dreamy inventor, but practical workman. All the time he had been toiling with his brain, others had been toiling with their hands. Before he had :;ompleted his invention, the engine house was built, the engine installed, a lathe fixed up and a brick furnace erected. Two practical mechanics were engaged, and everything was ready fox the fitting together of the machinery before the whole design had assumed a definite form. Directly Jordison's brain had accomplished part of its task, the work of construction commenced, and the framework of the car was completed before the finishing touches had been put to the plans for the machinery. Every week castings came in from the various firms with whom the orders had been placed- These were filed and finished off and fitted together in the workshop. In less than three months from the date when the first castings had been thrown into the creek, the car was completed, and Jordison sold his so h.p. Jacquart for Lsooo. _ _

On October 25th, Jordison took the first run on his new motor. It was blowing half a gale, pouring with rain, and the roads were deep in mud and water. It was a severe test for the new car, but she mine through it splendOly, and ploughed through the storm like a shic through a heavy sea, throwing up a shower of mud, like spray, on each side of her. Jordi• son revelled in the ride. The wind and rain lashed him like a whip, but he drove through it all at the top speed, and gloried in the powel of his new-found toy. 1-le was an experienced motorist, and knew before he had gone half a dozen miles that no one had ever driven such a car as this before.

For three hours he sat with his hand on the steering wheel, and in that time they had traversed Essex' from North to South and East to West: Lipp sat shivering and cursing by his side. He was there to learn all about the monster that jumped and quivered be- neath him. He was commencing his educa- tion as a chauffeur. But he only took a feeble interest in the proceedings, and while jordison explained the art of driving, his whole mind was occupied with wondering when the car would be scattered in pieces over the roadway. For, like many experts, Jor- dison cut his corners very close indeed..

Lipp's face did not brighten until they came within sight of the Red House. The ugly building on the little hill had never appeared in so attractive a light to him before. No mariner returning from a stormy voyage could have welcomed the first glimpse of home with greater joy and thankfulness.

Ten , ..as they rushed along the straight road, the hill in front of them was suddenly hidden in a flash of blinding light. A few seconds later a loud report burst on their ears, and tie ground trembled beneath them. Instindlively Jordison put on the brake, just as a man shuts his eyes to protect them from danger, not stopping to reason whether he will come to harm or not. The great car slowed down, and peering through the driving rain, the two occupants saw a heavy cloud of smoke pouring across the marshes, and long tongues of lire leaping up from the

"The dynamite," said Jordison hastily. A large supply of this dangerous material had been stored near the engine house. Jordison had proposed to blast out a cave in the solid rock close to the road, where he could keep his motor and a large store of petrol. „ .

"I've 'ad enough of your cursed motor," growled Lipp. "I only wish it had been in the shed, and Gawd bless the dynamite then, I say. I'd like to see it in smithereens." Jordison smiled sweetly. Then he released the brake, pulled the lever towards him, and the car glided forward.

" You- will get used to it, Lipp," he said, "and there's always a chance of its going to smithereens, as you so aptly express it. A foot too much to one side or the other at 90 miles an hour will do a lot to gratify your desire."
" Motor folk are a pack of -- fools," rejoined Lipp, clinging to the side of the car, as Jordison purposely drove one wheel withiu an inch of the bank.

"I would not worry if I were you, Lipp. You have got other things to think of to-day. The petrol is all ablaze. I hope the house has not come down. Can you see anything ? " Lipp leant forward and glared at, the• hill, but it was still hidden in smoke and flames.

"Nothing," mumbled Lipp, " I only hope its killed Susanson, the :ittle swine," In less than five minutes the car came to a Standstill at the gate. The wind was from the south west, and the smoke was carried away from them, but it hid the 1-ed house from view. Jordison did not much care whether anyone was killed or not, but lb: was very thankful that the car was finished, and that it had not been blown to pieces in the explosion. A large supply of petrol had been stored in the engine house. That very afternoon he had intended to remove it to a. safer place. It had now removed itself, and in all probability most of the engine house as well. He had no desire to plunge into the thick and awful smoke and investigate matters. He sounded the horn on the car a dozen times and waited for information.

_ In two minutes' time Jenny appeared round the bottom of the hill. He was black with Oily soot from head to foot. His right cheek was bleeding, and, he limped. "Well, Jermy," said jordison, nis there snuch damage done ?
