Mr. GEORGE WYND• THE MACDONNELL HAM'S statement in the DEBATE. House on Tuesday cer- tainly failed to clear up the mystery of his relations with Sir ANTONY MACDONNELL. He denies that he had any sympathy with Devolution, or with any of the political ideas of Lord DUNRAVEN or the Under- S ,cretary. But he has made it no less inexplic- able than it was before why he had not nipped their ideas in the bud. Mr. WM' O'BRIEN said quite justly that Mr. WYNDHAM ought to have repudiated the Home Rule tendencies of his coadjutors before they had passed into the stage of public discussion.' The late Chief Secretary blames himself for not having 11 noticed what the organisers of the Land Confer- ence were striking at. It is the most extra- ordinary thing of all that he did not know what his Under-Secretary wanted—what his Under Secretary thought Mr. WYNDHAM knew all the time. It seems that Sir ANTONY MACDONNELL wrote a letter plainly setting forth what he had on his mind. Mr. WvxnuAm says he cannot remem- ber the letter, but he admits that Sir ANTONY, receiving no rebuke, had a right to assume that his policy was approved. This is certainly a very singular story. Mr.WYNnuAm knows nothing of the letter, Mr. BALFOUR knows nothing of the letter. Brit neither ventures to suggest that the letter was never sent. That Mr.WvNnitem should have forgotton a document of such importance transcends all the most notorious freaks of the official brain. It is curious that Ministers attach no blame to Sir ANTONY MACDONNELL. They did not use the word " indefensible " in speaking of his policy a short time ago,but that expression was hastily abandoned. He is treated with respect not unmingled with a little wholesome fear.

Sir H. CAMPDELL•BANNERMAN suggested that when Mr. WYNDHAM resigned there was no logical reason why Mr. BALFOUR did not go too. But the real b ign fic au ea of the situation is Sir ANTONY MACDONNELL remaining in spite of the Ulster Unionists. He paid a visit to Galway, and made it his business, in the course of his inquiries to interview the local bodies. Why the Under- Setretary, making a tour in Ireland, should not collect the opinions of local politicians who happen to be Nationalists, as pretty nearly all the politicians in Galway are, we have not the least idea. Ii he had not taken this course, he would have neglected his duty. But for a Castle official to have any dealings whatever with the Nationalists was an unpardonable offence in the eyes of the Orangemen. It is not an offence in Mr. BALFOUR'S eyes, and he has to suffer for his breadth of vision by losing the votes of the Ulster men in the House. These men are signally lacking n the best qualities of citizenship, and cannot forgive those who are better citizens than them- selves. Their method of maintaining the Union is to cut off from all share in the administration of Ireland every representa- tive of the great majority of Irishmen. Mr. BALFOUR disputed this priruiple of government by keeping Sir ANTONY MACDONNELL at his post. But how long will the Primo Minister show this firmness? He would not keep Mr. WYNDHAM.. That sacrifice did not content the Ulstermen, who demand that the Under-Secretary shall go too. Already there are hints in the Ministerial journals that Sir ANTONY MecDoNNELL cannot be retained in the face of this clamour. But the question is whether Mr. Bersoun,by dismissing Sir ANTONY, would not provoke that tenaciouo; official to reprisals. The Under• Secretary has not told his story, and if he should be free to tell it the upshot might be worse for the Government than any risk they run by flouting their Orange critics.

Though St. Austin's Ward bye-election resulted according to anticipation and Dr. Joseph was returned by a large majority the Labour men cannot be considered to have done badly. Mr. Horrocks was late in the field, had few workers, and issued a somewhat unwisely conceived election address, yet he obtained 245 votes. The fact has also to be considered that St. Austin's Ward is new ground for Labour, and that Dr. Joseph obtained a large amount of miscellaneous support, much of which might not be available under other circumstances. Gener- ally speaking, Labour made a plucky fight aganst odds, and need not be discouraged by the adverse result of the election.

There is a light: side to political work, and the Liberal party in Warrington is fortunate in pos- sessing helpers who are, perhaps, second to none in the arrangement of social functions. The concert hold at the Liberal Club on Thursday evening was voted to be unexcelled in the history of the club. For tbe time being the large billiard room had undergone a transformation at the hands of the manager, ai.d;the.fine array of plants which mot the eye of the visitor on entering re- minded one of botanical gardens. A high-class programme was listened to with manifest pleasure by a large audience, and the whole-hearted enthusiasm which pervaded the proceedings' served to strengthen the confidence of the local leaders in the forces at their command. The event of the evening was the presentation of billiard prizes by Mr. A. H. Crosfield. The prospective candidate is never happier than when speaking in encouragement of wholesome recrea- tive pursuits, and he recounted with a glow of pride the achievements of Warringtonians in the athletic world. A stirring address by Mr. Vivian brought home the political import of the occasion, 'arid should stimulate the workers to even gri-Ater zeal in the splendid causes for which Liberalism stands.

The 27th annual meeting of the National I Liberal Federation is to be held at Newcastle-on- -ITyne on the 18th and 19th instant. Two of the resolutions deal with Labouri and the Unemployed, viz.:—" That this Council s strongly of opinion that immediate steps should be taken to restore to workmen the right of effective combination of

which they have recently been deprived by decisions of thn Courts ; " "This Council is also of of opinion that the State should create permanent machinery applicable to the whole country for investigating and alleviating the lack of employ- ment caused from time to time by exceptional trade depression." How different from the attitude of our political opponents

Mr. Chamberlain, that arch-deceiver of the people, has been complaining of the "gross mis- representations of opponents" in the course of a letter in which he re-iterates an oft-exploded fallacy. " To listen to these critics," he proceeds" one would suppose that a trifling duty of 2s. a quarter on corn, which is less than the ordinary fluctua- tions in the price, and corresponds to less than one farthing per loaf, would reduce the people of this country to starvation, and that it was to our interest to allow the foreigner to enter our markets and compete with our workers without paying anything at all towards the rates and taxes of the country.'

We like the cool way in which Mr. Chamber- lain speaks of a 2s. per quarter duty on corn as "trifling," and in one sense we agree with him. It is " trifling " with the food of the people. In all protected countries the duty imposed has been small to commence with but it has speedily grown to be oppressive. If 2s. per quarter is sufficient to keep out foreign grain it will be sufficient to cause a shortage in the first necessity of life, for we cannot grow here all the grain we re- quire. If . the duty is sufficient to bai: foreign grain from our markets, then what ' advantage is it to the producer P In either case, ' the 2. or the additional amount which Mr. Cham- berlain's supporters are clamouring for, will have to be borne by the people who consume the food. Mr. Chamberlain also,declares that the duty would not increase the burdens of the people beyond one farthing per loaf. Even this is a farthing too much and would mean in many families 6d. per week on the food-bill. There are many ways of procuring revenue without further taxation of the people's 'food. As to the foreigner paying the tax, Mr. Chamberlain is once more conveniently unmindful of the view expressed in the House of Commons by Mr. Ritchie, a late Tory Chancellor of the Exchequer. The latter has unhesitatingly said that a tariff of the sort described by Mr. Chamberlain as "trifling" must fall upon the people of this country. No amount of specious argument will alter this fact, and it should never be lost sight of by the voters, for whose palates all these highly-seasoned fallacies are specially prepared.

Has a wife a vestei interest in her husband ? This seems to be the question—and a puzzling one too—arising out of a compensation case which has just been decided by Judge Bowen Rowlands after careful consideration. The claim is made by a widow who had been deserted by her husband a few years prior to his death, and the respondent's contention was that as she was not dependent upon her husband at the time of his fatal accident and death she was not entitled to compensa tion. His Honour has decided in favour of this view, and the widow therefore gets nothing. We hardly think the decision is an equitable one. Though the applicant 'was receiving no contribu- tion to her support from her husband she never- theless had in our opinion a sort of vested interest in him which possessed a pecuniary value. There was always the possibility—as long as he lived— that he might return to her, but that possibility has been destroyed by the man's untimely end. The applicant is therefore the loser by her husband's death whether she were dependent or not, and it seems to us that some monetary compensation is due to her in respeceof this loss.

A good solid fright is one of the best antidotes for indifference that a nation can have, but it is not good that the shock should ne too often ' repeated, and with too little excuse. Just now Iwe are suffering from an epidemic of shrieking prophets of evil. No sooner have we recovered from the horrified amazement induced by " C.B.'s" revelations in the" Daily Graphic "about defective guns th.in we are bronght up short on the other side by a, writer in " Blackwood's " who declares that our present' naval policy is ,the forerunner of national disaster, and that we cannot hope to have a thoroughly efficient fleet unless we revert to the condition which prevailed during the Napoleonic wars. Then comes Sir Cyprian Bridge, with further comments on the dangerous tendency la the lack of continuity which he conceives to be ' the chief feature of the Admiralty operations ; and our cup of terrors is filled by Lord Ellenborough, who shows how all our important harbours might be blocked, our fleets surprised, , and our navat strength set at naught by an enterprising enemy with little ingenuity. This sort of thing is all ' very well, but it is apt to make the ordinary man impatient. It is not surprising if there are those who regard these sensational outbursts with the philosophic doubt which proved the undoing of the shepherd in the story who cried " Wolf I" when there was no wolf. ,

Procession.

The celebrations of Warrington's victory in the Northern Union Cup Final will be continued this (Friday) evening, when there will be a procession of illuminated cars. The prccession will start from the Town Hall at 8.30 and on the first car will be the victorious team and the officials while Crosfleld's, the Volunteer and the Borough Bands will be in attendance. The cars have been been beautifully illuminated and will present an unusuallypleasing spectacle—a spectacle which will probably be improved by the presence of cyclists in costume. The following is a table of the times at which the procession will arrive at the various termini :

Leave Town Hall -30 arrive Sankey -50 „ Sankey B-50 „ Rylands-street 9-10 „ Rylands-street 9-10 „ Latchford 9-30 „ Latchford 9-30 „ Mersey-street. 9-15 „ Mersey-street 9-45 „ Cemetery lO-5 „ Cemetery lO-5 „ Central Station 10-20 „ Central Station 10-20 „ Jockey Bridge 10-30 „ Jockey Bridge 10-30 , Wilderspool ... 10-55 The members of the team, officials, and members of the committee, were on Saturday entertained to dinner at the Lion Hotel by Mr. W. R. Neil, a very enjoyable evening being spent. On Tuesday evening the cup- holders and the Lancashire Combination Champions were entertained by Mr. B. Lakes of the Blue Lion, and on the 23rd instant the team will be the guests of Sir Gilbert Greenall.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

MEETING 'Or THE PAROCHIAL COM ITTR E.—The annual meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Com- mittee was held in the schools on Thursday evening. There were present :—Messrs. G. Pilling, F. Warburton T. R. Westbrook, F. Pearson, W. Mclntyre, S. F. Welsby J. H. Clarke, J. Fairhurst, H. J. Westbrook, J. W. Bouchier, J. Hallows, J. Swinton (surveyor), and J. F. Ashton, (clerk). Mr. Hallows proposed the re-election of Mr. G. Pilling as chairman:of the committee. Mr. Pilling was a good and fair chairman and moreover he had what was wanted—influence on the District Coun- cil—and could do a great deal for the village. Mr. Pearson seconded, remarking that Mr. Pilling as a chairman was all that could be desired. The proposition was unanimously carried. Return- ing thanks Mr. Pilling said that all he could do to further the interests of the parish he would do.—On the motion of Mr. Pilling seconded by Mr. Welsby, Mr. J. H. Clarke was unanimously re•elected vice-chairman of the committee.—The Building, Sanitary and Lighting Committees were re-elected ; Mr. J. Mounfield was appointed chairman of the Building Committee ; Mr. Bouchier was elected chairman of the Sanitary Committee.

DINNER AT THE SARACEN'S lIEAD.—On Thursday evening Mr. J. H. Clarke entertained the members and officials of the Stockton Heath Parish Council and Parochial Cciinmittee, and a few friends, to dinner at the Saracen's Head Hotel, upon his retirement from the chairmanship of the Parish Council. An excellent repast was served to which about 25 sat down. The remainder of the evening was spent in conviviality, speechmaking being pleasingly interspersed with song. The usual loyal toasts were honoured on the proposition of the host. "Our Parish" was proposed by Mr. H. J. Westbrook, and rosponded to by Messrs. F. Pearson and J. Hallows. The health of the Parish Councillors and members of the Parochial Committee was drunk on the proposition of Mr. F. Howard, Messrs. J. W. Bouchier and G. Piling responding. Other toasts hououttd were "Our officials " and "The clergy and ministers of all denominations."

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

The burgesses of St. Austin's Ward were asked to Tote for Councillor Dr. Joseph.—" Because Dr. Joseph pays on an assessment of £143 per annum; because Mr. Horrocks only pays on an assessment of £9 per annum." We now know whether wealth and position count for anything in the Conservative party. * * The L.R.C. have again come into conflict with a valuable member on the question of personal liberty. Mr. J. Harker, the Labour candidate for North-East Manchester, has resigned owing to the fact that he is unwilling to accept the mandate of the local L.R.C. forbidding him to speak from the platforms of the Free Trade League. The L.R.C. appears to be steadily alienating the very men who are indispensible if labour representation is ever to grow out of the puling infant stage.

•* * * Is the Mersey getting purer? For we notice that a rowing club has been formed in the town. Twenty years ago, 64 pastime of rowing was extensively indulged in by the young men of Warrington, who found the upper reaches of the river far from unpleasant'. We have, ourselves, splashed an oar on: the turbid waters much more recently, but the experi- ence was not encouraging. Either the promoters of the new club must be less fastidious or the river is improving from the sportsman's standpoint. * * *

"Ours is a policy of common-sense as well as of sentiment, and I have entire confidence in our ultimate success." Thus Mr. Chamberlain in a letter t the ladies of the Tariff Reform League. We can only say that the "sense "is extremely common and that the "sentiment " lacks sympathy. People must be ever on their guard against the kind of sentiment which will increase their difficulty of Making both ends meet and may sacrifice the inestimable privilege of cheap , food.

* * * We heard a good story the other day of a War- rington' Alderman who contrived to get the better of a London cabby very neatly. The Alderman has an intimate acquaintance with distances and fares in the Metropolis and after a journey he handed the Jelin a two-shilling piece, which was in excess of the legal fare. Cabby thought he might spring a little more out of the " old gent" and remarked suggestively" This is not right, Is it sir ?" The Alderman quickly replied "Oh no, I see I have given you too much "—and promptly deducted sixpence. We are told that even language failed the cabby ! I *—* - -

The Women's Liberal Federation has held its annual meetings during the past week. There were about 1,000 delegates present,representing 567 Associa- tions with a total membership of 76,000. Mrs. Edmund Osborne and Mrs. Simpson, the delegatet. from our Liberal Associatian, were the guests of Mrs. Allan Baker of Dormington, Harlesden. They will doubtless be able to give a good report of the work of the Federation, as many interesting and instructive debates took place. It is pleasing to note that sixty- seven new Associations have joined the Federation during the year.

Those who live strenuously are naturally interested in the Simple Life. They will, therefore, listen to what Dr. Macnamara, the scholastic M.P., lms to say pertinent to the subject : ". It is of no use talking about the Simple Life until those who haVe it ia their power to set the fashion,set it in that direction. Until week-end house parties take sxlvan constitutionals instead of iced champagne, retire to rest at eleven instead of retiring from bridge with the dawn, eat three courses instead of thirteen, and dress in modest homespun instead of in satin-lined and velvet, these others will vote the Simple Life the worst of bad form."

The metaphorical octopi; is abroad in the land once more—if we may be e±cused for transporting it from itsi natural watery element. A short time ago there was a Stockton Heath octopus discovered by Mr. IL J. Westbrook. Now, a new type, "the octopus of industrial progress" has been found in the "Dawn." We don't doubt its genuineness in the least but wø feel bound, on its behalf, to query "the inky poison which its ever-growing arms exude." No octopus known to natural history ever did mrything so ua-natural or un-octopuslike. The love of metaphor seems to be leading some of our local htterat, tirs astray and we would suggest that they give the octopus a rest until they have obtained a closer acquaintance with its characteristics.

* * * the maxi otsvealth is by no means -2t.eivena ' grata with the Warrington Town Council, or, probably *4 with the bulk of the inhabitants. Millionaires are disapproved of. In fact we may almost say that .1 Warrington frowns on them, principally because they themselves have never smiled on Warrington. But Carnegie the business man, the man of energy and astuteness, is an individual with an opinion of some weight. Alluding to the tariff question in the course .1 of an interview the other day he said : —"I must tell you how pleased lam to see that that British Govern- 1 ment has just repudiated Chamberlain's policy. 'A dangerous oman that "—shaking his head— a danger" ousman. But that danger, at all events, has gone. The very fact of his failure makes for a closer union. i between the two great branches of our race." * * * .' .J The Raunds shoemakers have, with the help of several Members of Parliament acting on behalf of the A workers, succeeded in making themselves heard,as the following official statement, issued on Wednesdays ,'- indicates :—" It having been suggested to the Secre- wry of State for War that action should be takea under the fair wages resolution in reference to certain War Office contracts for army boots, he has determined ' so cause immediate and special inquiry to be made , whether there is at the present time a rate of wages accepted as current in certain portions of the county of ' Northampton for the various processes of army boot ~ manufacture, and, if so, to report what is the rate for each process? in their march to London, they were "models of behaviour" and they were complimented on their orderliness. We hope that their eaniestnese will excite in the minds of the Ministers some sympathy ; and that their demands will be conscientious-li - considered.

* * * We could almost smell the burnilig brimstone and feel the sulphurous fumes suffocating us as we read portions of Mr. Philip Snowden's speech which he delivered at Bradford on Sunday last. We had thought, that such Christian places as heaven ' and hell were purely imaginary. I3ut, after all the exple- tives which issued from Mr. P. Snowden lye can readily recognise that whilst there nleY, not be places' yet there are certainly conditions which approach very near to the meanings I of the terms 'heaven' and 'hell.' This is what he ig ! reported to have said : 'We had a country which was ! the heaven of the rich and the idle and the hell of the poor and industrious ; where heavenly religion wag calculating selfishness making the best of both world by getting a fortune in this and relying on a vicarious sacrifice to get a good place in the next. We had tt people whose one end and aim was to rise to the heaven of material prosperity by sinking into a hell of moral damnation. Commercial competition wag the most inhuman and devilish deity at whose shrine the human race had ever worshipped.' Be warned in time !

* * * Mr. Henry Vivian, the Liberal candidate for Birken'„ head, is a Devonshire man with a fresh complexion, o keen blue eye, and a resolute chin. He is an old trade unionist, a member of the Amalgamated Society 0! Carpenters and Joiners, and was for some time presr dent of the largest branch of the Society in London. Like most " joiners " Mr. Vivian can hit the nail on the head, and hi his speeches there are no half-hearted or hesitating expressions of opinion. Industrial problems have long been his special study, and, increasingly so since he participated in the big joiners strike in 1891. An evidence of his keen interest in the workers is given by the fact that Mr. Vivian ;5 secretary of the Labour C&-partnership Assoeiatlon 3 body wllich is doing splendid service in bridging the gap between capital and labour. Already there arc' about 140 Co-partnership concerns in the countrY• The housing question also takes up much of 3lr• Vivian's time and he is chairman of the Ealing Tenants Limited, an association of tenant-owners wo-' have put their capital together, and are develor ing an estate and erecting houses of their own. Every man has a share of the increased assessable value resulting from the, enterprise, and once a tenant-owner he is always. 3 tenant-owner' frbe from fears of mortgage or depreela- tion, A Council has been formed to extend this scheme all over the country. Apart' from parti politics, therefore, Mr. Vivian is a busy man. 'lei 'however, is fighting the Free Trade battle with wig'', and main, and if the Birkenhead constituents do return him to the House of Commons they will neglecting their own interests and at the same tiroo be retarding the progress of a man who is bound to make his mark.

4‘ By POI ti:S we mean the business of Government, that is to say, the control and management of people living together in a soctetr."—Edward Jenks, MA. * * * Mr. Vivian on Wednesday described Protection as legalised brigandage.' We agree with him ; and believe that plundering' is a fine art in which the Tariff Reform Leaguers `are adepts. * * * • The Conservative Party has wrecked the Trades Disputes Bill. The amendment introduced by Mr. Galloway and carried by this " mugwump " of a Government indicates quite clearly their attitude towards the workingmen. Everyone who is worth anything carries his higher nature with him into his Politics but we are now satisfied that the members of the present Government leave their higher nature with their constituents and carry their other with them into the Roo- tf Co-

* * The axiom that " A bird in the hand is worth two 'Tithe bush" appears to have impressed itself on the mind of a son of toil who was called to give evidence in a County Court case on Thursday. He entered the box with a business-like air, aud the usher prepared to administer the oath. Before that functionary could 'commence the usual formula, the witness, with a suspicion of alarm in his voice, inquired " Will your Honour grant me costs at the, close of the case ?" The Court was amused, but the Judge assured the wifness that the point would be considered- at the, 3proper time. No doubt a" cash down" system would be a much appreciated innovation at the Court.

Tram Accident. An accident, happily not attended with serious con,- sequences, occurred on Monday in Bridge-street. A Runcorn dady, Mrs. Cooper, was crossing the street when she failed to notice a tramcar approaching, and she was knocked down. The driver immediately stopped the car. Mrs. Cooper was at once removed to the Infirmary, where it was f mud that her injuries were not serious.

Rowing Club Formed. At a meeting which was held at the Ring-o'-Bells, Church-street; on Monday evening, it was decided to form a Warrington Rowing Club. Mr. E. Gibson was elected secretary and treasurer, Mr. J. Newton being appointed assistant hon. secretary and treasurer. Mr. William Brimelow was appointed captain, Mr. P. Ditchfield sub-captain, and Messrs. G. Platt, E. Lunt, and H. Brimelow were elected to form the committee. UNDER THE.CLOCK for Good BOOTS.—Advt. Inquest on a Child. Mr. Brighouse, County Coroner' held an inquest at the Police Station on Mqnday on the body of Edith GilkS, the three-weeks-old daughter of John Gilks, warehouseman, residing at 9, Pierpoint-street. The evidence showed that Mr. and Mrs. Gilks -retired to bed as usual on Friday night, taking the child Edith and another child aged two with them. On waking next morning Mrs. Gilks found the baby dead wtth the elder child lying across its face. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

Speaking at the inauguration of the work upon a new factory building at Birmingham to-day, Mr. E. A. Wilson the chairman of the New Hudson Cycle Com- pany Ltd., said that " Although the building of this particular new factory was amply warranted and urgently demanded by j.he very great expansion of business caused by the exception illy low prices of bicycles this season, it was a matter of some doubt how long these low prices could Continue. On all hands, the prices of the materials used in bicycle manufacture were being advanced. Pneumatic Tyres had gone up in consequence of the continual rise in the price of rubber, whilst steel in all its forms and particularly in the form of steel balls Ind weldless tube had recently greatly risen in price, and it was consequently difficult to sea how the corresponding advance upon the pri6o of the bicycle could be long delayed.!' , I The -Late Mr. A. H. Dunn. - - --

_ Appropriate • reference to the late Mr. ,A. H. Dunn is Made in the current issue of "The Warrington Circuit Wesleyan Methodist Church Record.' "Mr. Dunn" says the Record "has taken very much interest in the Church Record," attending to all the financial work in connection .with it, giving no small amount of time and energy. There was another piece of work that he has done for the Circuit, which very few know anything about, but though requiring great care and accuracy, was always accomplished in a most excellent fashion. It was the dempiling of the Circuit Chapel Schedule which has every year to be prepared for the Synod. It is not our intention to write an obituary, but we must be allowed to say how much we admired his honesty, candour, • fearlessness, and capacity and readiness for work. In his latest hours, as in earlier ones, his faith in the Saviour gave him peace and confidence."

The quarterly meeting of the Sunday School teachers asiociation was held in St. James's school on Monday evening. There was a large attendance over which the Rev. Morley Stevenson presided. Mr. John Littler Runcorn, read a paper on "The increasing import- ance of Sunday School work at the present time." Mr. Littler pointed out the importance of Sunday Schools in view of the possible danger of the Church losing the day schools. Ile also strongly advocated the teaching of boys over 15 years of age by men instead of by ladies,said strong efforts should be made to instruct the children in the faith of the Church. He agreed with teachers giving the children work to do at home, because as much attehtion should be given to Sunday schbol work during the week as on Sunday. He suggested that the clergy should help the teachers. (Applause.) An interesting discussion followed. Votes of thanks to the chairman and speaker con- cluded the meeting. PUBLIC BENEFIT. UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LA.NCASIIIRE.—Advt. Embezzlement , by an Army Pensioner. At the Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, Alfred Lamb, Leonard-street, Stockton Heath, was charged with.embezzling £5, the money of Messrs. R. White and Sons, Limited, mineral water manufacturers. Mr. Browne, who prosecuted, stated that the prisoner had been in employ of the firm at Newton Heath, Man- chester for sixyears. He was an army pensioner, and seven weeks ago he was brought down to London Bridge, Stockton Heath, to manage the local depot there.. He had only been there seven weeks when Mr. Fitzgerald, the cashier for the firm, on going through the accounts found that defendant was £5 Os. Gil. deficient in cash in his accounts. After some ques- tioning prisoner admitted the offence and said the money had gone in drink and household expenses. The object of the firm—who employed no fewer than :300 carters in London alone—was to warn other employees. The prisoner's wife had been to see him that morning, rind she had informed him that she had six children, and that if there was a conviction in this case the pension would be lost. The firm felt that if the prisoner lost his pension—which amounted to £l4 a year—the punishment would be too great and they had, therefore, consented, with the permission of the Bench, to allow the prisoner to pay to the firm the amount of the pension in July. In these circum- stances he asked the Bench to adjourn the case for two months, £3 to be paid into court in July., He (Mr. Browne) would take his clients' instructions and practically withdraw the case.—The Bench adjourned the case for two months.

div.head: Unknown Man's Suicide.
div.p: Unknown Man's Suicide.

Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at the Chapel House Inn, Burtonwood on Saturday,on the body of a man unknown which was found hanging from a beam in an out building iii the rear of Dallam Farm, Burtonwood. —The evidence showed that at about 7.45 a.m. the previous Thursday, Michael Naughton, went to the shed and there saw the body of a man hanging from a beam. He called the assistance of another labourer on the farm named Henry White who looked in the shed and went and told Mr. Warburton, the farmer. All three took another view, but did not venture near the body, only to feel that man's hands, which were cold. Mr. War- burton set off to Padgate Police Station, a distance of 3I miles, where ha informed P.S. Mellor, who arrived on the scene at nine o'clock. The sergeant at once 'cut the body down and found it was still warm, although the hands and feet were cold. Artificial means of respiration were employed for half an hour, but without avail. The Coroner said he had very little doubt that if the body had been cut down when first dis- covered the life would have been saved.—P.S. Mellor : I asked Mr. Warburton why he did not cut the body down, and he said "You have to be very careful nowadays. I thought I had better let the police see him first."—The Coroner: How long is this supposi- tion that people are not entitled to cut down a body until the police have seen it going to last ?—The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide," there being no evid-1 ence to show the state of deceased's mind at the time. The following is the police description of the deceased: —About 26 years of age, five feet five Inches in height, light brown hair, slight, prawn moustache, grey eyes, . dressed in dark grey overcoat,black jacket and vest,hlack trousers with blue stripe and patent leather boots. From the discoloration of his hands, the police believe lie was a eh rnical worker.

(Applause). He thought they who were connected with that club ought to record their admiration for the prowess of the Warringtonians who achieved that magnificent victory in Leeds the other day. (Applause.) He would not attempt to recite to them the category of field sports and athletic events in which Warrington had cut an uncommonly good figure. He really thought the •-town which had always been considered exceptional in possessing a greater variety of industries than any other town in the country had another distinction in having, perhaps.won laurels in more fields of sport than any other town in the kingdom. (Applause.) At any rate he was certain no town of the same size as War- rington had done so well. We bad made the highest mark in football, and their old friend Mr. Charles Hutchings, who used to be a Warringtonian, had won the championship of golf. In cricket his own family bad done a little—(hear, hear),—and they had a very distinguished cricketer (Dr. Smith) present that night who showed that be was equally useful at billiards. Warrington had done remarkably well and he could only repeat that it vies aflne thing, because a man could not get the first place in the field of sport unless he kept himself in what Emerson had described as the top of condition. Athletics had also a fine moral effect upon our race. The only thing we had to take care about was that while we thoroughly enjoyed our games, we did not shirk the greater and more im- portant issues of life, and played our part as good citizens in every capacity. He hoped Mr. Vivian's brief address would have its effect, and that they would think it worth while in the cause of good government and genuine progress to get rid of much of the flashy clap-trap we had had in politics for some years past, and see that a healthier tone and a better influence pre- vailed politically in Warrington than had been the case for the past generation. div.head: BISCUITS.
div.p: BISCUITS.
WARRINGTON
PHOTOGRAPHIC SOCIETY.
SECOND OPEN EXHIBITION.

Those ardent camera enthusiasts who comprise the Warrington Photographic Society have every reason to congratulate themselves Upon the gratifying success of their second open exhibition which has been held in the Museum Art Gallery this week. Progress in a commendable 'work is the outstanding impression derived from the exhibition. A year ago the Old Academy sufficed to provide the necessary accom- modation, but on the present occasion the more corn- modious Art Gallery has proved none too large for i the display of the very numerous pictures—in fact its capacity has been taxed to the fullest extant. ' The tone of the exhibition marks a dis- tinct advance. Fine specimens of work from nearly all parts of the country are to be seen, and photographic postcards have come from as far north as the Orkneys. Some of the photographs which for the past few days have adorned the walls of the Art Gallery were exhibited at the Royal Photographic Society's last exhibition—notably those of Mr. John Hepburn and Miss Mary C. Eames. As to the highly creditable character of the exhibition as a whole, we cannot do better than quote the opinion of t4e judge (the Rev. Henry W. Dick, of 'Manchester) who stated: —" Considering that this exhibition is Only the second open competition hell by the society, I consider that the support given has been generous, and that the quality of the work on the whole is distinctly good. The architecture and figure studies are exception- ally strong, and altogether the show will have a stimulating effect upon the local worker's." . . _

The vale of the exhibition from the latter stand- point can hardly be over-estimated. It, should be the means of encouraging a friendly rivalry amongst local amateurs, while it also affords them an opportunity of seeing how their work compares with that of more experienced outside competitors. The total number of exhibits is about five hundred, and as may be imagined the task of hanging the pictures was not an easy one. There was certainly room for improvement in this direction and it would have been much more convenient to the visitors had the pictures been placed in consecutive order according to their numbers. The prizes, it ma 7 be stated, consist of plaques,specially designed by Frank Knott, for the most meritori- ous photographs 7 and certificates for those which are entitled to rank second.

div.head: PRIZE PICTURES.
div.p: THE PRIZE PICTURES.

The open classes have been excellently supported,and the exhibits are such as to well repay inspection. In the landscape, seascape, and river section, Mr. James Ashurst, a native of Warrington, was awarded a plaque for his "Where men toil "—a picture which should appeal particularly to Warringtonians. It depicts a grimy centre of industry, with chimneys belching forth clouds of smoke, and Mr. Ashurst has succeeded in pro- ducing an artistic effect from very prosaic surroundings. The photograph, which is one of exceptional merit, obtained a medal at the Edinburgh exhibition. Mr. Ashurst has also an exceedingly clever figure study— "A Scotch fish wife," portraying a typical caller of the herring. Mr. To mkinson,an equally successsul competitor in!this chit's, is to be complimented upon his study "The glory of the silent eve "which conveys a fine idea of expanse and solitude. One cannot help contrasting it with "The end of the glacier" (Dr. C. Thurstan Holland) which hangs immediately above and shows the icy debris, splintered into all manner of fantastic shapes, which has been swept down from the mountain by the glacier in its course. The two pictures are vastly dissimilar and yet both rank high in the same class. There are some very striking specimens of portreiture, figure and flower studies. Mr. John Hepburn isl deservedly successful with "When once life's day draws near the gloaming" —a sepia-toned indoor study which is full of feeling. The subject of the composition is a placid-looking old lady, with shawl and cap,sitting contemplatively, book on lap, by a cheerful fire, above which a kettle is sus- pended in the old-fashioned way. Mr. Albert E. Coleman, who was also awarded a plaque in this class, shows "The dinner hour; A game of nap "—the sub- ject, as the title suggests, being a group of rugged workmen deeply engrossed in the fascinating card game. The fruit study (white currants) by Mr. E. Seymour, end " Chrysanthemums" by Mr. D. NV. Kyle obtained certificates and are both splendidly-finished examples of this particular class of work. The most striking feature of Mr. Kyle's photograph is the admirable way in which the soft and delicate texture of the flowers is brought out. The architectural class is exceptionally strong and the judge was so impressed with the excellence of the exhibits that three plaques were awarded. The success- ful pictures are distinctly creditable. Mr. William A. Clarke's "An abode of ancient peace" shows the interior of an old Church with the sunlight streaming through the latticed window. ,The great beauty of the work is the soft and yet contrasted effect of sunlight and shadow. In "A shaft of light" Mr. G. S. Kimber has embodied a very similar idea. Here the gloom of a crypt is suddenly d spelled by al bright] gleam of sunshine through a deeply embrasured window. Mr. S. L. Coulthurst, a well-known exhibitor, was also a prize winner with "An arcaded street." This unique scene has an almost tunnel-like effect, the lightstriking through from above at odd intervals. In the lantern slide competition Mr. E. Seymour's "fruit study' is perhaps the most striking exhibit and certainly merits the plaque awarded. The texture of the leaves and transparency of the white currants, as shown in such a small photograph, are really . remarkable. Mr. F. G. Tryhorn's" Evening of life" a pleasing study, and in this interesting class certificates were awarded to Messrs H. Wormleighton and IV. H. Goy. The society made a new and commendable departure this year in offering prizes for the best collection of photographs of "Old Warrington." Unfortunately the response did not involve a competition, as Mr. James Harding's collec- tion being the only one sent in. It is due to Mr. Harding to say that his series is highly interesting and obviously the result of much labour. It presents views of old local landmarks, some of which have disappeared with the modernizing of the town. For instance there is a photograph of a monument which formerly stood at the end of Orford-avenue; and the old lodge at Bewsey and Lodge-lane are shown. Another 1 interesting picture is a view of the weir at Latchford, showing in the background the Parish Church before the 1 square tower was replaced by the present graceful spire. In another section of the exhibition Mr. Harding has a truly artistic photograph of the Acker's Pool, Latchford, which is worthy of mention. To the average visitor to the exhibition the section devoted to photographic postcards will probably be even more attrac- tive than the nicture classes. The display ie exception- ally good, and the variety should prove suiflcent to interest all. Mr. Fred Judge secured the plaque for a very pretty card—" Roses "—marked by the naturalness of the tiowers,andgreat delicacy of treatment.lklr.Arthrir Smith, who was °awarded a certificate, shows a fine hetidstudy, in warm brown, of an "Old Salt." A col- lection of sea-scapes, forwarded ey Mr. T. Kent of the Orkneys, includes some remarkably fine cloud effects and the series greatly enhances the interest of this class.

Totem to tha members' classes, the entries are hardly so numerous as might have been expected, but the exhibits without exception reflect credit upon the Society. It is to be regretted that full advantage was not taken of the committee's offer of a framed or un- framed picture for members who had not previously taken an award, for owing to insufficient entries no awards were made. Mr. Kenneth F. Bishop is to the fore in the landscape, seascape, and river scenery class, and obtained a Ware for a very pleasing ' study " Birches," showing graceful trees shooting perpendicularly from a rich under-growth. The photo- ; graph embodies an excellent perspective, but in our view ' the effect would have been improved by the trimming lof an inch off the foreground of tho print. It may be stated that Mr. Bishop gained the prize in Mr. Fair- hurst's recent local competition, with the same work. Mr. W. H. Podmo re's "Are you ready ?".a very meritorious I study, is a notable success in the same class. It I depicts a tired pedestrian taking a rest, while a dog , looks appealingly into his face, as if to ask him to resume the ramble. Mr. Daniel S. Birrell's "Brown's Bay, Ireland,"—a typical Irish landscape, I with cattle and whitewashed cottages as fore- ground objects—was awarded a certificate. In the section for portraiture figure and flower studies Mr. Kenneth F. Bishop arid Mr. Henry Bond were each awarded plaques. Mr. Bishop has made a feature of urchin studies and his "Sun bath "—a iiew of a ragged infant sprawling on the flags in the full blaze of the sun—is a particularly good example of his work in this particular line. At this point it may be noted that Mr. Bishop's "A windy corner" in another part of the exhibition, while not receiving recognition from the adjudicator, is well worthy of special mention. It proves that Mr. Bishop possesses the artist's eye in addition to considerable command of technique. Ti, return to the portraiture class, Mr. Henry Bond was successful with a portrait in profile, which is very rich in half tone. The architectural class produced good work, and the awards were obtained by Mr. George Nicholls and Mr. Daniel S. Birrell (plaques) and Mr. Fred Gidinan (certificate). Mr. Nicholl's "Time worn" depicts a rugged Norman archway fully described by the title. Mr. Birrell exhibits an effective picture of an old stairway at Haddon Hall, while Mr. Gidman has a most interesting view of an elaborate Norman arch at St. Bee's Church, Cumberland, in which a remark- able amount of chisselling is clearly and softly defined. A capital collection of lantern slides adds further interest to the exhibition, Mr. Henry Bond securing first honours with " The bridge at Arley "—a charming rural scene. As showing the fascinations which photography has for old and young alike,it may he mentioned that Mr.Thoinas liesketh,who is over eighty years of ago and is still an active devotee of the camera, afforded the society the privilege of ex-

div.head: LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: LIBERAL CLUB.
MR. A. H. CROSFIELD DISTRIBUTES THE BILLIARD PRIZES.
Warrington's Athletic Achievements.

One of the most successful and enjoyable social functions ever held at •the Liberal Club took place on Thursday evening, the occasion being the distribution by Mr. A. H. Crosfield of the prizes gained in the Christmas and New Year billiard handicaps. Thanks largely to the efforts of Mr. E. A. Sanders, a smoking ' concert had been arranged, and a really excellent pro- gramme was submitted. The recent departure of inviting ladies to attend was again acted upon, and the large response was evidence that the innovation was highly appreciated. The largo billiard room was admirably suited for the function, and taste- ful decorations produced a pleasing effect. Plants and flowers were arranged on the billiard tables, and when the room was filled a very bright scene was presented. An excellent chairman was found in Alderman Tinnion who prefaced the concert with a brief address. Owing to the Liberal meeting in Whitecross Ward, Mr. Crosfield did not arrive until late in the evening, and on entering the room he had a very cordial reception. He was accom- panied by Mr. H. Vivian, the prospective candidate for Birkenhead, Mr. C. E. Parker, .and Mr. Joseph Howes,while amongst others present were:—Councillors Wilkinson, Maginn, and James Evans, Dr. R. Smith, Messrs. C. Jackson Holmes, A. Browne, W. Furness, P. Garnett, J. Worrall. and T. Pemberton. THE CHAIRMAN'S SPEECH.

In his opening remarks the Chairman expressed the great pleasure it afforded him to see so many ,ladies present and to know that they were taking an interest in the social side of political work. Although they had not votes, the ladies had a great influence, and he was glad that so ninny of them rendered active assistance as members of the Women's Liberal Asso- ciation. He hoped all the ladies present, whether they were members of the Association or not, would do their utmost to bring aboUt aLiberal victory at the next election.(Applsuse),ln his opinion,there never wasa time when politics were of more importance to ladies If the proposals of Mr. Chamberlain were carried into effect, the ladies, to whose foresight so much of the comfort of the home was due; would regret not haying opposed them more strongly, as lie felt sure that, With- out any adequate compensation. Protection would raise the mice of £1 worth of goods to 255. They had long hoped to return a Jaeral member for Warring- ton and they had often been disappointed. ,They con- fidently hoped that the next time would pay for all and that Mr. Crosfield would be at the head of the I poll. (Applause.)

div.head: CONCERT.
div.p: THE CONCERT.

A most enjoyable musical programme was then pro- ceeded with. Songs were rendered in a highly creditable manner by Miss L. Fairlthrst, Mr. P. J. George and Master Griffiths, and the Lyric quartette party delighted the assembly with several selections in which the voices of the vocalists blended with beautiful effect. Miss A.!Woodland and Miss Fairhurst gave a bright and artistic interpretation of a duet. Mr. R. H. Pearson added much to the pleasure of the evening with two violin solos executed in masterly style, and Mr, W. Rutter is deserving of praise for excellent cornet solos. Mr. E. A. Sanders once more supplied the humour, and his recitation in the Lanca- shire dialect provoked a great deal of mirth. Mr. W. H. Payton, Mll9. Bac., and Mr. A. 'Prow ably dis- charged the duties of accompanists.

THE PRIZE DISTRIBUTION. MR. CROSFIELb ON THE VALUE OF OAMES• The CHAIRMAN, in calling upon Mr. Crosfield to dis- tribute the prizes, expressed the great pleasure which it afforded them to see him present,and thanked him for his generosity in presenting the prizes. Mr. CROSPIELD delivered a short speech. He observed that people said at times that he took too much interest in games, either by playing them himself or encourag- ing others to do so. He was bound to say he had never had any qualms of conscience on the point. He believed that games were a means to an end, and he thought it was a great pity when people made them an end in them- selves. There were very much more important things than games, but still he felt -..ery strongly that games had an immense amount to do with the formation of English character. He thought there was a vast deal of truth in the saying of the late Duke of Wellington that was quoted to him when he viewed the picturesque grounds of Eton College the other day, that the Battle of Waterloo was won in the play-grounds of Eton." Mr. Crosfield paid a tribute to the excellent

Mr. F.G. Taylor presided at the third of the series of lantern lectures on rhursday evening, the lecturer being Dr. Thurston Holland. President of the Liverpool Amateur Photographic Association, who described some of his travois 'in Switzerland. In introducing the lecturer, the Chairman remarked upon the great work Dr. Holland's knowledge of photography had enabled him to do in connection with the profession of which he was so distinguished a member, the Exhibition being enriched with a series of radiographs showing various diseases and accidents to the bone which were awarded the medal of,the Royal Photographic Society last year. It was for work of that character that the Society, had honoured themselves by electing Dr. Thurstan Holland a member. Dr. Thurston Holland then pro- ceeded with his lecture which was illustrated with as fine a collection of photographs as it has been our lot to see, the lecturer-being endowed to an eminent degree with the ability to impart much of the pleasure he had himself derived from a holiday amongst the mighty f Alps. Descriptive notes of a highly instructive and 1 entertaining character gave much pleasare to the large
of."

div.head: GRAPPENIIALL
div.p: GRAPPENIIALL

THE enicKET CLIJR.-0 wing to the enthusiasm evoked by the final for the Cup a fortnight ago, the village club only commenced their fixtures last Saturday, when they paid a visit to Widnes, having opponents in the White Rose. Ideal cricket weather prevailed. The homestors opened the innings but only knocked up 29. Warburton and Watson shared the honours of the bowling. The visitors replied with 50. Banks played a capital innings for his 20, Ellis being second with 12. The fielding on both sides, was particularly good. The 2nd eleven. had as visitors Sankey Wire Mills and easily disposed of them. The wire Mills have, evidently, not got into their stride, 17 being a very poor total to make- Grappenhall 2nd put together 59 runs. J. Albinson and John Burrows bowled to some purpose, the former taking 7 wickets for 11 runs and the latter 3 for G. The same pair wielded the bat successfully scoring 10 and 12 respectively.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

FOUR Mos Tits FOR NOTORIOrS THIEF. "The most notorious thief in Warrington" was Superintendent Monaghan's description of James Taylor who was sentenced to four months imprisonment at the Borough Police Court on Saturday. Prisoner was charged, along with a woman named Elizabeth Smith, with stealing a skirt from the shop of Mr. T. Dorhville, pawnbroker, Knutsford-road. A further charge of assaulting Police Constable Clarke was preferred against Taylor, while the woman was also charged with having been drunk and disorderly.—The evidence showed that P.C. Clarke saw the prisoners enter and leave the shop of the prosecutor. There was something bulky beneath Taylor's jacket, and knowing his reputation, the Constable searched him and found the skirt concealed. On being taken into custody, prisoner became very violent and struck out right and left. The woman escaped but was caught by Mr. Charles Ashton, of the Bridge Inn, who rendered valuable assistance to the, officer.—The woman denied having been concerned in ' the theft, and, in a statement to the Bench, Taylor accepted full responsibility—Taylor was sent to gaol for four months, while the Bench gave Smith the benefit of the doubt in the theft case. For drunkenness she was fined ss. and costs.—Mr. Ashton was thanked by the magistrates for assisting the constable.

A. COSTLY JOKE. Albert Harris, a stranger, was charged at the War- rington police court on Monday with stealing a piece of beef value 3s. 6d. the property of Mr. Wainwright, butcher, Buttermarket-street. The Chief Constable stated that on Saturday night the prisoner was seen by P.C. Armstrong to go up to the shop window of Mr. Wainwright in a suspicious manner. He approached in a crouching attitude three times and the third time the „officer saw him" coax " a piece of beef to the edge of the counter until it fell off into his hands. Prisoner immediately put the beef under his coat and walked away. Armstrong stopped him when the prisoner said "It is all right officer it is just a joke, Prironer said he was one of the men affected by the Nottingham boot strike and bad come to Warrington in search of work. Mr. William Roberts: It is apity you came so far with your "larking."—The Chief Constable : Perhaps no one could see the point of his jokes nearer than Warh rington. Prisoner was sent to gaol for Ft days wit bard labour.

div.head: ALLEGED UNIAWFUL WOUNDING,
div.p: ALLEGED UNIAWFUL WOUNDING,

At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, before Alderman Hutchinson (presiding), and other magistrates, Mary Harris, 15, Pierpoint-street, was charged with assaulting her husband on Monaay afternoon with intent to do him grievous bodily harm.—Superintendent Monaghan stated that the prisoner's husband was a hairdresser. They had been married a number of years but had lived unhappily through drinking and quarrelling. Atone o'clock on Monday the prisoner went Into the house drunk and asked her husband for some money for drink. He refused and she then threw a beer bottle at him but missed her aim and he then went up- stairs. Prisoner followed him, and it was supposed she picked up the leg of a chair and struck him on the head. I The police got to know about the affair at night, and Sergeant Barnett and P.C. Heap went to the house. They knocked several times and the prisoner eventually I came to the door and said: " Don't kick the whole neighbourhood up." They found a large quantity of I blood on the bed, and the prisoner's husband was at -once removed to the Infirmary, where he was found to be suffering from loss of blood. The prisoner was arre:ted, and when charged, said: "Itis an untruth.'4 Prisoner was remanded until to-day.

div.head: Warrington Borough Police Court.
div.p: Warrington Borough Police Court.
Minor Cases.

310NDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alderman Smethurst, Councillor Wilkinson, Messrs. Hayward, Thornton, Pilling, and W. Roberts. THE BEGGING NUISANCE.—John Santlow, a stranger to Warrington, was charged with begging in Palmyra- square on Saturday afternoon.—Upon his promising to leave the town he was discharged.—William Ashton, Tanner's-lane, was charged with begging in Scotland- road on Saturday night.—P.C. Hewitt said he saw the prisoner in Scotland-road accost several persons. He followed one man and witness heard him say he would not go until he got a penny.—Prisoner was fined ss. and costs (12s. in all) or in default seven days' imprisonment with hard labour. . FOOTBALL IN THE STREETS.—Sidney Fellows, 295, Liverpool-road, William Farmer, 192, Liverpool-road, Arthur Silvers, HO, Liverpool-road,and Percy Hamblett, 15, Barry-street, were charged with playing football in Evelyn-street ; and were each fined 3s. tid.—The Chief Constable remarked that he had received a large number of complaints of lads playing football in the streets. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—John Salt was charged with illtreating a horse on the 28th April.—lnspector Gibson of the R.S.P.D.A., stated that on the date in question the defendant struck the horse about the head and gave it a running kick under the stomach. When witness examined the horse he found a wound on the rear fore leg two inches in length and three-quarters of an inch in width. Defendant was in the influence of drink at the time. Under ordinary conditions he treated his horses very well indeed.—A fine of 13s. in the costs was mposed.

TETE RUNCORN SENSATION. The boy Fred Walker, aged ten years on remand on a charge of attemptinr, to murdez Ethel Gatley, aged three years, was brought before Mr. Imison, at Runcorn Police Court on Wednesday, Superintendent Ennion said he had visited the house where the girl was being nursed. She was doing fairly well, but was still in bed and would not be able to leave her bed for some time He asked for a remand for another week.—The prison e ivas reminded accordingly,

THE DUST PROBLEM.
Experiments on the Road Near
Knutsford.

The dust nuisance is a growing evil on our country roads, the growing popularity of motors in every form having rendered the problem a serious one for road surveyors and County and District road authorities. But dustless roads are now within the bounds of possibility and the Cheshire road surveyors are taking a great amount of intsrest in the all important ques- tion of Dust Prevention. On Friday and Saturday last a stretch of road just outside Knutsford on the Holmes- Chapel-road was treated for a distance of 1.200 yards with a new Patent Composition recently introduced by a Liverpool firm. On the first day a demonstration was given in the presence of Messrs. B. S. Newcombe (Warrington District Surveyor), A. Linnell (Cheshire County Council District Surveyor), and John Brooks (Northwich Urban District Council Surveyor). The Surveyor for the Enutsford Urban District Council also inspected the work. Messrs. J. H. 13-synes, J. F. Ward, F. C. Hunt, E. J. Lowe and J. Richardson (corn- mittee men Manchester Motor Club) were also in attendance, while a well-known motor journalist who has made the subject of dust prevention his especial study watched the experiment with interest. The new Dust-laying Compo may be described as a Liquid Asphalt. ft is dark in colour, and is sprayed into the road surface to the depth of half-an-inch by a 1 suction and force pump at a pressure of 50Ibs. to the ' square inch. It binds the surface material of the road and its effects are claimed to last six weeks, keeping the road free from mud or dust and rendering road watering unnecessary. If a second coating is applied at the end of six weeks the effect will be more lasting than the I first treatment. It costs £4 per ton and five barrels goll to the ton, which quantity will efilciently treat over half-a-mile of road, so that it is much cheaper than other similar preparations. The experiments were very satisfactory.' The road treated is clean with a healthy disinfectant odour and is very cool and refreshing to travel over after the usual dusty white road. A fast motor car driven at full speed raised a perfect cloud of white dust which stopped and hung on the very edge of the treated portion of the road only to rise again when the car reached the un- treated part of the road at the other end. All who travelled over it were loud in their praises of the new dust laving c unno. The road was finished on Saturday and Motorists-Cyclists and other road users who travelled over it were extremely gratified. The total cost works out at less than a farthing per square yard. The experiment will be watched with keen interest and will be compared with other preparations which have been tried and proved successful dust layers and pre- ventatives. The great points of course is the length of time the effects of such road treatment will last. The Compo is a valuable disinfectant as well as a Dust pre- ventative.

div.head: ECHOES IN THE WAR.
div.p: ECHOES IN THE WAR.
A Widow's Trying Ordeal.

div.head: TRANSPORTER BRIDGE.
div.p: THE TRANSPORTER BRIDGE.
Unofficial Trial Trip.

On Tuesday afternoon, Mr. John J. Webster (chief engineer of the scheme), Mr. L. H. Jhase (resident engineer),and Mr. F. El. Stables (secretary to the Bridge Company) were the chief passengers on what was said to be an unofficial trial trip of the car of the IVidnes and Runcorn Transporter Bridge Company. The passage from Runcorn to Widnes occupied 4 mins. 10 secs. This could have been easily reduced by the application of more power, but the test was not for speed but smooth- ness of working, and Mr. Webster deolarecl it, quite satisfactory. There was very little sense of motion,the merely gliding to Widnes. The return journey was also accomplished without the least hitch. The car is a platform 55 feet long by 25 feet wide, and is capable of holding four 2-horse waggons loaded and 300 passengers. There is a shelter for passengers. The bottom of the car is 12 feet above high water level, and it clears the ship canal wall by 4 feet G inches. The motive power is electricity. The car is saspended by steel wire reibes from a trolley 77 feet long, which runs upon rails on the underside of the girders of the bridge. The trolley is carried by sixteen wheels on each rail, and is propelled by two electric motors of about 35 horse power each, the electricity being generated by a 70 horse-power gas engine on the Widnes side The car can be brought up within its own length when travelling at full speed. The regulation time for crossing the river is 21 minutes.

div.head: Sunday School Anniversary.
div.p: Sunday School Anniversary.

The Sunday school anniversary in connection with Bewsey-road Church was celebrated on Sunday by the olding of special services of which the preacher, morning and evening, was the Rev. J. Grange Bennett, connexional evangelist, formerly of Warring- ton. The rev. gentleman preached in the morning to a large congregation, his subject being " Casting out dev, Is," dealing with the evils it was necessary to tight against in these days. In the evening Mr. Bennett spoke of the importance of people givin,, themselves to His service. In the afternoon, a spacial musical service was given by the children and choir. Mr. John E. Richardson presided, and spoke upon the excellence of the work carried on at the mission in Silver-street by Messrs. Robert Wood and W. Parkinson. He said it was a pleasure to him to help forward the cause they had so much at heart. A feature of the service was the anthems rendered by the choir and the hymns which were beautifully sung by the children, under the con- ductorship of Mr. Williams. Mr. Wadsworth prosidedat the organ, and the collections for the day !amounted to which it is expected will be made into £5O by friends who were unable to be present.

div.head: ST. AUSTIN'S WARD ELECTION. --- Dr. Joseph's Large Majority.
div.p: ST. AUSTIN'S WARD ELECTION. --- Dr. Joseph's Large Majority.

By a majority of 314 Dr. G. W. Joseph was on 'Mon- day returned to represent St. Austin's Ward in the Town Council until November next. The bye-election was keenly contested, Dr. Joseph, who was the Conservative candidate, being opposed by Mr. E. Horrocks, the nominee of the Gas Workers' and General Labourers' Union. Mr. Horrocks's candidature was endorsed by ' the local Labour Representation Committee. Very little election literature was circulated. Dr. Joseph declared himself a dEtermined advocate of economy, and stated that he was of opinion that every step possible should be taken to further reduce the high rates. He would, ho said, give careful considera- tion to efficiency and progress in the management of the affairs of the Borough. With regard to the vital necessity for absolute probity in publio work, he was opposed to any member of the Council benefiting in any way from his position. A poster issued on Saturday contained the following letter from Mr. James Dodds, in support of Dr. Joseph's candidature :—Dear Dr. Joseph,—ln every respect I look upon your candidature for the vacant seat in the Town Council as an ideal one. I congratulate you upon it and upon your address, and if necessary I will do all in my power to secure your triumphant return. I can- not believe, however, that you will be opposed if you are, I shall be sorry for your opponent. Your courageous and self-denying action will prove, I cannot doubt, an incentive to other gentlemen of education and standing in the town to follow your example, in which event the ratepayers may confidently look forward to the moral and intellectual tone and character of our local administration being immensely raised, and to the affairs of the County Borough being wisely and economically conducted. With best wishes, yours faithfully, JAMES DODOS. Mr. Horrocks, in his address, informed the electors that he believed in absolute purity of government, and further stated that he strongly favoured a further extension of municipal enterprise, trade union rate of wages, and an eight-hour day for all Corporation work- men, direct employment of labour by the Corporation, the feeding of under-fed school children, abolition of all insanitary property under the Working Classes' Dwellings Acts, free education, immediate construction of a healthy and commodious lodging house on modem principles, free baths, cheaper gas, branch libraries, useful work for the unemployed, taxing of land values, a stringent Fair Wage Clause in all Corporation con- tracts, reduction in tram fares. Public meetings had been held by each candidate, and there was a large number of workers on either s.de. The polling stations and officials were as follows:— Cairo-street school, presidin,, officer, :I,lr. A. Starkey, poll clerk, Mr. Samuel Wright; Thewlis-street school, presiding officers, Messrs. H. Lawrence and W. H. J. Jenkins, poll clerks, Messrs. Doug.las Skelton and Walter Sumner. Out of 1,116 persons entitled to exercise the franchise, only 801 voted. At the Cairo- street school, pAling was very brisk between the hours of eight and ten in the morning. The number of votes recorded at Thewlis-street throughout the day was com- paratively small.

div.head: VIE RESULT.
div.p: VIE RESULT.

At eight o'clock in the evening the polling booths were closed, and the ballot boxes were conveyed to the Town Hall. The counting was expeditiously carried out in the large committee in the presence of the presiding alderman (Alderman Bennett), the candi- dates, several members of the Town Council,anclot hers. Alderman Bennett declared the result as follows at half past eight : Dr. G. W. Joseph Mr. E. Horrocks
Majority

Dr. JOSEPir moved a vote of thanks to the presiding alderman and officials for the part they had taken in the election. He felt the election had been well fought and, moreover, honestly and pleasantly fought. He bad nothing. but the best of feelings towards his opponent, and, although he was successful, he must say that he respected Mr. Horrocks and the sentiments that gentle- man had shown towards him.

Mr. E. HORROCKS said the fact that he was in the position of a defeated candidate made it somewhat awkward for him tie second the vote of thanks, but, nevertheless, it afforded him pleJsure to do so. He did not mind being defeated. As Dr. Joseph had said, they had fought comfortably together,and he sincerely hoped the memories of the election would rest with Dr. Joseph and all those concerned, as a very quiet and sociable election.

The vote was heartily carried. Alderman BENNETT, in acknowledging the compli- ment. said his part in the election had been very slight and very plclsant. He wished he could congratulate both candidates—(laughter)—but he could not do that. He congratulated the winner very heartily and condoled with the loser. He could only re-echo what both the speakers had said—that the election had been fought in a particularly friendly spirit which was creditable to all concerned.

div.head: TEIE PUBLIC DECLARATION.
div.p: TEIE PUBLIC DECLARATION.
A large crowd assembled to hear the declaration of the result from the Town Hall steps. The figures were received with cheers.

Dr. JOSEPII said he was delighted to be in the position of successful candidate. He thanked the electors very cordially for their support, and concluded by saying that he would do his best to fulfil the promises he had made. (Applause.) Mr. HounocKs said it afforded him great pleasure to say that Labour had again secured somewhat of a victory. For the first time in the history of St. Austin's ward, Labour had contested the seat, but with very poor weapons indeed, and in his belief, Labour played a very remarkable game. It was not the last time they would contest the Ward. (Applause,) He had not a word to say against their opponents, who had been very well equipped for the fight. It had been a case of every man to his g .r- -ticular duty, whereas with regard to the workingmen, how could they possibly enter into the work of the election like their opponents ? The election had been fought honour.iblv. They hid done their best and stated their belief, and, to all intents and purposes, as far as the workers were concerned, they wore perfectly satisfied with the result. (Hear, hear.) He sincerely hoped that if there was a Labour candidate at. the next election they would rally round him in the same 'way and do Labour the great honour of electing a representa- tive. (Applause).

div.head: AT TEIE CONSEBVATIVE CLUB.
div.p: AT TEIE CONSEBVATIVE CLUB.

The news of the victory was received with enthusiasm at the Conservative Club. Addressing a gathering of workers in the first class billiard room, Dr. Joseph said they had won a big victory. The election had been well fought and had it not been for the good support he had received, the majority would have been very small. Ho could not sufficiently thank all those who had rendered assistance. One th:ng the elec- tion had done, was to prove that he had a great many more friends than he thought. (Applause). The election had hem a pleasant one, and he had not seen any acrimony or bad feeling on either side. Ho desired particularly to thank the chairman (Hr. W. Gill), Hr. Richardson, Mr. Edwin Woods, Councillor Fulton-Smith and the members of the com- mittee.

Air. W. (km: also delivered a short speech and said he was sure that in retnrning Dr. Joseph they had placed the right man in the right place. (Applause.) Special thanks were due to :qrs. Edelsten for her help.

The committee were consequently in a dilemmaand it was decided not to contest the seat. div.head: WESLEYAN METHODISM.
div.p: WESLEYAN METHODISM.
Liverpool District Synod at Colwyn Bay.,

On Monday, the May Synod of the ministers in !the Livertiool district of the Wesleyan Methodist Church commenced. at Colwyn Bay. For the first time the Synod thus assembles on the North Wales coast. .When the place of the May assembly for this yeir came to be fixed last year, an invitation came from Chester, and was accepted. Bat the unpleasant discovery was made that the meetings would have to be held in the Chester race week, and a cordial invitation coming opportunely from Llandndno. Rhyl, and Colwyn Bay jointly, it was at once accepted. Hospitality for the ministers, 130 in number, was readily obtained by the local committee. The guests during the w eak have included some 200 lay representatives. The district comprises the circuits , along the coast from Morecambe in the north to Aberys; twyth in the south, excepting the Welsh Wesleyad churches which form twos districts to themselves. The following local ministers have attended :—Revs. G. H. Carnson, R. Wilkin Rees and J. Manning (Warrington), Ralph Green, W. Terry Coppin and William Jackson (Runcorn), Edwin Gelder (Frodsham), Charles D. Newman and John Pickup (Whines), T. Wheatley, Alfred S. Sharp and W. A. Prunell (Chester). and Thomas Hollis, F. R. Smith, John Horn, and Harold W. Perkins, (St. Helens) and Prescot). Warrington people will be interested to learn that the Rev. Frederick Payne, who, during the years 1855 to 1858 was one of the Wesleyan ministers in Warrington, was, in 1886. the first superintendent of Colwyn Bay circuit. THE WEIGHT OF CROWDS.

In" Molesworth's Pocket-Book " we ("Engineering") and it stated that, for rough calculations of the loads of bridges, 120 lb. per square foot may be taken for the weight of a crowd of people; while in " Trautwine's pocket-Book " we are told that a suspension bridge should not have a factor of safety of less than three against, a load of people, whose weight is taken at 10010. i _ per square foot, which includes an allowance for wind, and for the crowd being in motion. Many years ago, Ithe engineers of the Chelsea Bridge had a number of I picked men placed on the table of a weighing machine, land packed together as close as possible. It was then found, continues " Engineering,' that a load on the table of 84 lb. per square foot was produced. Another result, corresponding with that given in " Molesworth's Pocket-Book," s‘..l obtained by Mr. Hart, archite3t of Buckingham Palace, who had men wedged together as closely as possible on an area 20ft. in diameter. This gave a result of 120 lb. per square foot. -Quith recently. however, Professor L. J. Johnson, of Harvard University, showed that under certain con- ditions it is possible to obtain much higher figures than those we have mentioned, for he has carried out experi- ments which show that a loading of 1501 b to le,olb per square foot may be produced by the weight of an assmibled group of persons without undue crowding ; and later experiments on similar linos showed that with a maximum condition of loading, or one in which forty pioked men were placed on an area of 06 square feet, a load of 181.31 b per square foot was obtained. This is of course, an extreme figure, and could only be obtained with picked menial:id Profesior Johnson states that they were all tall and carefully selected. The average weight of each man was 163 lb. The men all faced in one direction, a position which favours close packing ; but, adds engineering, itis a condition of things that might easily occur naturally in a crowd. •

div.head: Coal Dealer Fined.
div.p: Coal Dealer Fined.

At the Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, Olbin Emmess, 20, Sutton-street, Warrington, coal dealer, was summoned for having on March 21st, at Stockton Heath, offered opal for sale which was of less weight than that specified upon the label attached to the sacks.—Roger Hind, inspector of weights and measures for the County Council, stated that he saw the defendant, together with his man, delivering coal in sacks to houses in Stockton Heath. When he went to the lurry he found upon it 38 sacks of coal. He weighed each of the backs and out of the 38 he found 21 were deficient in weight to a total extent of 1651b5. Defendant produced the delivery note explaining that he had not got it with him at the time he was with the cart. The Chairman of the Bench said that as this was the first offence the defendant would be fined 10s. and costs but he must remember that this was a very serious offence because poor people were being defrauded out of coal. If another similar case came before that Court serious notice would be taken of it.
