div.head: [ALL MOATS AIRSERTBD.
div.p: [ALL MOATS AIRSERTBD.
LORD TENNYSON'S BAD FIVE MINUTES,
TrIE REV. GEORGE W. SKENE (Author of" 7e Bishop's Ghost Story," to.).

A Poet Laureate's life, like that of the pro- verbial policeman, is not always a happy one. There are moments when the lustre of an ac- credited pre-eminence in the world of rhyme And metre is tarnished, and the deathless bay leaves are powerless to comfort. It seems, per- Imps, a little unfair, and we could; no doubt, have managed it much better ourselves, but, under the normal constitution of things, the life that charms is not necessarily itself a charmed one, and certain awkwardnesses come to Poets Laureate as to others. One of the late Lord Tennyson's experiences in Paris was an excep- tionally awkward one. It illustrates the truth that a little learning is a dangerous thing, and may serve as a warning to those whp, re- gardless of idiom and accent, breezily adventure themselves into unknown tongues. On re- flection, the warning seems rather to be against travelling with those who do, for Lord Tenny- son was the victim here, and his knowledge of the language was never, in question. Where could be found the hardihood to suggest that a Laureate was capabl9 of speaking anything but the most perfect French 2 Indeed he spoke it volubly, very volubly on this occasion, reveal- ing intimate acquaintance with those more lurid profundities of speech, which the fine phrenzy of an infuriated tongue alone can reach. To call for hot water, or to ask one's way in the street, is the stock in trade of any Cook's tourist : but to elaborate a joke, successfully to negotiate that prevarication to which rude people apply a shorter word; above all, to give fitting expression to feelings of overwhelming indignation in terms " understanded of the people,' is to scale the loftier heights, to rank as h Past Master of the vernacular. In this last• qualification the Laureate was without reproach.
A WIILL *FAXING FRIEN-D.

But his friend 2 For he had a friend with him, and that was what made the trouble. To be saved from one's friends becomes occasionally a spontaneous petition'. This friend was a close relative, Professor L., and the two had gone to spend a few days in Paris together. On their arrival, they secured rooms that suited them, two bed-rooms and a sitting-room, in one of the pleasant Boulevards. The weather was cold and bracing, and their first demand was for a fire. With the table drawn,up close to it, as he felt chilly, Lord Tennyson 'presently sat down to write, facing the door; and the Pro- fessor, knowing that his companion had, to write against time, said he would leave him un- disturbed, and go out for a stroll. Downstairs he remembered having noticed that the basket of wood, which is the Parisian substitute for coal, was empty; and calling to the house- porter. who was sitting in his glass cage by the 1. entrance, he told him in what he believed to be French, not to let the fire go out. The porter sprang up to attention, saluted, booked the I order, and the Professor, returning the salute. walked steadily away, without a suspicion of what evil times he had left behind him.

Meanwhile, Lord Tennyson wrote on, till by and by the creaking of the door arrested his attention •, looking up, he saw that ,j,t was be- ing stealthily opened; and a face peered in on him. He made a gesture of impatience, and the face was hastily withdrawn. But the mental thread of continuity was broken, and the writing lagged. Duringi those pauses, which all who attempt to write under such conditions know but too well, he caught himself wonder- ing what that lace at the door could have meant, when with a start he detected another there. There was menace in the eyes too, and he distinctly heard muttered questionings and whispers outside. Any interruption is annoy- ing when even minutes are precious, but such an interruption was beyond all endurance. He rose abruptly, in undisguised anger, and made swiftly for the door, intending to slam it in the face of this impertinent intruder, and to lock it.

div.head: AN ANGUY PO ET.
div.p: AN ANGUY PO ET.

But before he could reach it, it was flung wide open, and, to his amazement, he saw two gend- armes, behind them the house-porter, and be- hind him again a little crowd of terrified persons in the various stages a incipient flight. There was a pause, an awfnl pause. Then the vials overflowed. That expression is as good as any other, for the deluge of wrath, which sent the timid following ilyingjound the corner, beggared all description. The stalwart three, alpne re- mained, as. MitCaulay's heroes remained to hold the bridge " in the brave days Of old." These threeleld the door, as the torrent raged 'around them. They were cold, impassive men, and they stood there, significantly nodding at one another at every fresh explosion, though they did, no doubt inadvertently, close :up more and more as this now thoroughly exasperated gentleman continued to denounce them. At intervals he would ask them what this scandal meant, what law 111 E had broken that the police should trespass on him in this monstrous way. Did they know who he was? Did they know what he was? At this all three nodded, as if relieved that they were coming to the point at last. Well, and what does that mean ?" he asked. with sudden calmness. " Have you mistaken me for some criminal? Do you identify me as someone who has escaped from Astice 1' Then why don't you take me into custody? I am controlling myself with difficulty, but I want your answer. Who am I? And why are you here ? Speak, and at once, while I tun in the mood to listen. What brings you here ?"
" Monsieur answered 'one Of the gend- armes, " our instructions are not to take you into custody, but to prevent your leaving this room."
DIITAINPD UNDER SUSPICION.
" And why? In Heaven's name, why P" " This Monsieur " pointing to the house- porter," will explain." "Explain, then, you madman, and be quick about it."

"Pardon, Monsieur," began the porter, "but at'a it." " 'What's it?" " Monsieur has himself used the word." " Word? What word ?" "Madman I Monsieur's friend said that Monsieur was not to be allowed to leave the room."
=PAINED UNDER SUSPICION.

" Whikt P" thundered the astounded Laureate. " Madman Not leave the room ! You shall see. Stand aside. I command you," and he tried to force the passae in disdainful silence. The gendarmes blocked the way, and the spokesman urged. " Impossible, Monsieur, our instructions are clear. Monsieur will not compel us to use violence P"

"But I tell you it is a mistake, an absolute mistake. J am no more mad than you are. I Claim my liberty, and I will have it," and once more he made a determined attempt to leave the room. But to convince another of one's sanity, if he is beforehand convinced that one is mad, is., found on trial not so easy as it sounds. Both silence and speech are mist construed, both action and inaction are mis- understood, and the chances are that outraged nature will only so net as to confirm the con- viction. That is what Lord Tennyson dis- covered. A brief, one-sided tussle followed. and he found himself helpless in the hands of his tormentors, who were more than ever satis- fied that there had been no mistake as to the condition of their unhappy prisoner. He tried to reason with , them, he tried to frighten them with threats oT an appeal to the Embassy, he tried to bribe them, and finally with a sudden wrench he made a bold bid for freedom. But in vain. They were too qu.ck for him. With the skill born of practice they teste,ned his wrists together behind his back and strapped him co the handle of a heavy bureau, mounting guard one on either side of him ; and this was the spectacle with 1 which the astonished Professor was confronted on his return. By THE CLUBMAN.

A Touring Tip. It has always been a 'batter of some surprise to me why farms are not more patronized, in Preference to expensive hotels, by riders when touring. The delights of a stay, no matter how brief, at a good old- *fashioned farmhouse are lar ahead of anything that can be obtained at hostelries. I have found that there is always an absence of freedom—a lack of homeliness, as it were—about the matter.
of - fact system which

prevails hotels. At the farmhouse matters are very different indeed. In ninety-nine cases out of a hundred you receive almost a royal welcome, and regret is invariably expressed by the kindly farm-folk when the time Comes for your departure. On the other hand, some hotel .people are apt to look upon the tourist With his cycle as a bit of a nuisance, and the only time that the average Boniface looks pleasant is 'when you hand over cash in exchange for a bill of overwhelming dimensions. The farmhouse for 'billeting" purposes, when on tour, has the ad- ditional merit of being cheaper, and the quality of the food fresher, if simpler, than that supplied by the hotels.
WHICH SHALL IT BE-FARM OR HOTEL?

,I, 'Cycling' recently published a most useful list - ,of farmhouses where the wants of cyclists are I catered for, and such a step in the right direction I certainly a very acceptable and useful inno- ,. 'ration.
Improving the Club Run.

A much greater interest may be taken in the week-end club run where the riders have some object in view other than merely scorching to the destination, swallowing down a heavy meal and returning shortly afterwards on the home journey. Many villages and country towns literally teem With interesting sights and "show places," and visits to such places amply repay for the work of exploration. I have before me a note from the hon. sec. of a club, which although it is only in its infancy, evidently means to be enterprising and fully in accord with the poet Cowper, who declares that "variety is the spice of life." This club pro- poses to run a novel competition during the present season, which will doubtless provide plenty of fun, and at the same time possess the advantage of increasing each member's knowledge of various interesting subjects. The idea is that the members Will each write a paper descriptive of the season's experience, and the MS. may be either humorous, or of a general character, embracing historical rents. To the winner in each class a prize will be awarded. The example seems to me well worth copying. Cyclists who visit us from the United States spend
SEEKING OUT THE POINTS
EST.

'weeks before their visa in studying up the historical and literary associations of our country towns and rural villages; but the English cyclist too often takes no interest whatever in such subjects, and taisses one of the greatest pleasures of intelligent travel.

div.head: Back Wheel Adjustments.
div.p: Back Wheel Adjustments.

One of the best improvements in the details of Cycle construction, which has been carried out quietly and without any particular fuss by many Silas, is in providing exact means of securing correct adjustment of the back hub so that the clAin wheels are both in exact hue. This ensures 'the chain always running straight, true, and easily. There are several ways of doing this, but they all 'work on more or less the same plan as far as the rider is concerned. An index hand is provided on 41'1'14 forks and the hub works in a special scale. The figures on this scale have to be adjusted BO that the index hand on the back forks points to the saMe figure on the scale on both sides of the hub. When these agree exactly the index pointing to the .B.rne figure on both sides, it indicates the back hub Is Correctly adjusted, and the chain can be relied ell to run smoothly and sweetly.

Our illustration is taken from the patent adjust- Inent fitted to the New Hudson cycles as well as to 'flany other good makes. It is a pity that such a 'useful device is not of universal adoption. There Just one word of advice to be given the rider cting these devices. It is imperative both the %razes and the index be kept legible and free from blud and dirt, or they will be quite useless. A very difficult five stroke, a pot, and a. ball-top ball cannon)--Cue ball and red ball about 10 inches apart and exactly on a line between the middle of the centre pockets. Object white about 10 inches from the red and forming a right angle with the other balls.
JIo II

Diagram 97 shows a very difficult fancy stroke —a five shot made by potting the red and can- noning direct on to the white. Many players often state that such a stroke, with the balls accurately placed as shown on the diagram must be absolutely impossible, arguing that in order for the red to be potted it must be struck full in the face, and that if the cue ball catch the red full in the face it cannot cannon on to the white. Nevertheless a five stroke as shown on the diagram is quite possible, and many years ago John Roberts used to include it in his reper- toire of fancy strokes, though it was one that he always treated with great respect • The stroke is only possible to any player who can strike a ball tremendously hard, but given this qualification it ought to be made once or twice out of twenty tries. The cue ball must be struck with side—right hand side when the white is to the right of the red as shown on the diagram—but only a little below the centre, and aim must be taken dead full on to the red. Should the cue ball be struck low down so much reverse rotation would 1)e imparted to it, that it would recoil right back to the striker. fly striking the cue ball Only a little below the centre and with side, the 'reverse rotation is not sufficiently powerful to cause a straight-bark recoil. The cue ball by the strength of the stroke is forced a little ,beyond the point'of 'contact, and sometimes even an, inch or two past the spot which the red ball occupied, and then travels in the direction of the white ball, its path forming a curve as shown on the diagram. The reason that the cue ball describes this eccen- tric curve is because though the strong impact with the red has checked the forward movement of the rotating cue ball, the cue ball still travels on account of its rotation. This rotation at the moment of the cue ball's impact on to the red is neither round a horizontal axis as it would be were the cue ball struck with bottom only, MT round a nearly perpendicular axis as iE would be Were the cue ball struck with side only, but rather round an axis which is somewhere near the- mean between horizontal and perpen_ dicular.

In playing this stroke the cue ball after potting the red will generally pass the white on the inside, that is it will travel be- tween the white and the striker. Wheri this happens, too much reverse rotation has been imparted to thitball, and it has thus come back too much, even though it has not recoiled in a straight line, and the reverse rotation must be reduced by not hitting the ball quite so low. As before stated, the stroke must be played at a tremendous pace in order to drive the cue ball past its point of contact with the red. With the pace employed the red must be hit quite full, otherwise it will not go into the pocket. It is true that the pocket is much larger than the ball, but though this gives a certain amount of lati- tude when playing a slow pot, it gives prac- tically none whatever when playing at a very high pace, for unless the fast ball goes straight to the centre of the pocket it will bump out from one of the angles. Even though it strike the angle well past the fall of the slate, it will still be thrown back on the bed of the table.

div.head: HALF-BALL SCREWS.
div.p: HALF-BALL SCREWS.

In several books on billiards it is stated that the limit of a half-ball screw is a right angle, that is to say, that no matter how hard an object ball be struck and how much screw or reverse rotation be imparted to the cue ball, the angle of deflection cannot exceed a right angle provided that the object ball be taken half-ball. This id, however, theoretically incorrect, and only approximately correct in practice. When the cue and object balls are very near each other a strong half-ball screw quite destroys the right angle theory. For example, if the balls are placed on the bible in the position shown on Diagram SB—the cue ball being only one inch from

div.head: DIAGRAM 9&
div.p: DIAGRAM 9&

the red—a strong half-ball stroke (and with the object ball so near it is very easy to ensure half- ball hitting) will cause the cue ball to describe a pronounced curve, provided that the stroke has been played with plenty of screw. If, however, the strength of the stroke be reduced, the cannon may be made by means of a half-ball screw. (The explanation of the curve often described by the cue ball in strong screw strokes was _given two weeks ago.)

Wgen the cue ball- is some little distance away from the first object ball a right-angle screw is easy enough, provided that the object ball be taken half-ball. All that is required is a moderately strong shot and plenty of screw.

div.head: DEATH OF AN OLD RUNCORN FOOTRALLER.
div.p: DEATH OF AN OLD RUNCORN FOOTRALLER.

The death took place on Saturday, of Mr. William Faulkner, who was, for many years a well-known playing member of the Runcorn Football Club. He *tired three or four years ago,and for ten years prior to that did service in both the first and second teams. For some years he was captain of the first team and was also captain of Cheshire County. He was captain the first year litincom won the Lancashire Senior Competition. On several occasions ho played in North v. South and also for the Rest of England. He was accounted one of the best forwards the club ever possessed, and in the old Rugby Union days he was considered one of the finest forwards in the country. He excelled as a captain, and the team never played better than when under his control. Runcorn, writes "Philistine" in the "Athletic News," is mourning the demise of Will Faulkner, a well-known member of the club, cut off in the prime of life by that dread scourge consumption. When he finished his foot- ball career about six years a_go, anyone would have taken a lease upon his life. He was a fine figure of a man, tall, broad, symmetrical, with not an ounce of lumber, and though he had a giant's strength he did not use it like a giant. He was a sure and absolutely fair tackler, and never heard to wrangle. He was fairly speedy, a good kick, and a splendid passer, and he varied his transfer as be varied his forward play, and he had an unerring eye for an .opening. During his captaincy he exacted the utmost unselfishness from the players, and it was combination that kept Runcorn in the front ranktfor so many years. Faulkner was captain when, in the first season of the N.U., Runcorn carried off the Lancashire Championship after a historic struggle with Oldham on Broughton Rangers' ground. He was also captian of Cheshire County, played several times for North and South, and also for the Rest of England, but he never attained what he at one time fondly hoped for, an international cap.

LIBERAL ACTIVITY.
PUBLIC MEETINGS IN LATCHFORD AND WHITECROSS WARDS.
Speeches by Mr. A. H. Crosfield, Mr. H. Vivian, Mr. J. Howes and others.

Two successful meetings arranged by the Progres- sive LaboUr League have been held in the Latchford and Whitecross Wards this week, the principal speaker being Mr. 11. Vivian, prospective candidate for Birken- head: Mr. A. H. Crosfield has presided over each meeting and notwithstanding the summer-like weather there have been large attendances.

div.head: MEETING IN ST. JAMES' SCHOOL.
div.p: MEETING IN ST. JAMES' SCHOOL.

Foreign Policy and the Fiscal Question. The first meeting was held in St. James' School, Latchford, on Wednesday. Mr. A. H. Crosfield pre- sided and the attendance included : Mr. H. Vivian, Mr. C. E. Parker, Rey.. J. F. Matthews, Mr. Joseph Howes, Mr. and Mrs. C. Jackson Holmes, Mr. Edmund Osborne and Mr. J. A. J. Morton.
MR. CROSFIELD ON FOREIGN POLICY. THE ARMENIAN AND MACEDONIAN ARTROCITIES.

The CHAIRMAN said they were all very much indebted to his friend Mr. Vivian for coming down to pay them another visit. He had promised to speak to them that night and on Thursday on the great controversy on which the country was engaged, and he (Mr. Crostleld) was sure it would ill become Inrn in the chair to tres- pass on the preserves of his guest. He bad felt, as he dare say all his hearers had felt during these last few years, that we had been going through a PERIOD OF REACTION, and he wanted to read to them what had been said by a very able man who had written recently on the ques- tion. He would give them a few sentences from Mr. Hobhouse's summary of what he called the immense self-dupery of the Boer war,", not merely because his remarks had reference to that sad and anxious period, but because his opinions on a kind of false imperislism had a bearing on what had gone on in many parts of the world during that period of what he called democratic reaction. Little by little, Mr. Hobhouse said, it had become clear- er that the new Imperialism stood not for a widened and ennobled sense of national responsibility, but for a hard assertion of racial supremacy and material force." The unprejudiced observer was compelled to recognise that "judged by actual performance, it meant perpetual warfare, battles which, where black or yellow men were concerned, became sheer massacres, campaigns which, where a resolute white race stood in the way, involved , desolation unspeakable, the destruction of political and personal freedom, and the erection on their ruins of an un-English type of overpaid and incompetent official- dom, the cold-shouldering of the British immigrant, and the recrudescence of servile labour. Finally comparing the battle-cry with the actual result of victory, he began to ask himself whether the enterprises on which his fellow countrymen freely spent their blood were such as ministered to the glory of the Empire and the good of humanity, or rather to the vanity of a self- confident satrap and the lucre of a capitalist." Some months ago be (Mr. Crosfield) was travelling in •the East. and he had an opportunity of learning from I eye-witnesses on the spot and very competent judges,' some of the other consequences of the new and FALSE KIND OF IMPERIALISM. He was sure the meeting would not misunderstand him, and think he stood there to pose as what was called a little Englander, because he had never been a little Englander. (Hear. hear.) He thought there was a great tendency to depreciate what this little island itself had done; the wonderful men it had produced, the lead it had given to the world in liberty and in sound progress. But he did not think anybody who had crossed the water and seen that mighty kingdom of Canada or who had witnessed the admirable work that had been done by this country in developing the resources and improving the condition of Egypt, could fail to recognize that England had not only a great record in our own land but we bad done fine work in other parts of the world also. If they asked him to define—and leflnitions and names were often mislead- ing—he must say that for his own part, he very much preferred to think of the great British Commonwealth than to indulge in any of that flashy talk of which they beard so much, about the new Imperialism. (Applause). He must say he had learnt many very sad facts as illustrating some of the tenden- cies of that Imperialism. He was afraid they were in too many quarters a disposition to cringe to the strong and to seek AGGRANDIZEMENT AT THE EXPENSE OF THE WEAK. (Hear, hear.) That, he believed, was unworthy of our traditions in history, and of the character of English- men of which we were proud. Proceeding to deal with foreign issues, Mr. Crosfleld said that while they had terrible problems in our own land to deal with, and which they hoped—and hope was a part of Liberalism—(hear, hear)—and intended in due time to solve, he hoped they would not begin and end there. He hoped they would remember that in This little isle set in the silvery sea That serves it in the office of a wall we were in a favoured position, and it behoved us, as it also behoved that great Republic across the water, to stand shoulder to shoulder for more justice and better Government throughout the world. (Applause.) He had been brought up to believe that, but assuredly it had impressed itself upon his mind as it must impress itself upon the minds of anyone who saw THE FRIGHTFUL MISGOVERNMENT in that part of Europe where he had recently been travelling, and who realized, too, that after all England was not wholly irresponsible in the matter. Everybody heard in the years 1895 and 1896 of the fearful and inhuman treatment that thousands and hundreds of thousands of fellow-Christians of ours, to whom we were under some obligation, had to undergo in the East of Europe and in Asia Minor. He had been in touch with many eye-witnesses, Englishmen and Americans for whose word he could vouch—men in high positios, whose testimony they could not for one instant doubt— and he supposed the most awful tragedy which had resulted from iniquitous government in modern times ,bad been TIIK TRF.ATMF.NT OF THE ARMENIANS in Asia Minor. (Hear, hear.) Between 1895 and 1896, speaking in round numbers, no less than 150,000 of them were massacred in cold blood. He spoke to some of the responsible men who visited the country at the time, and asked them why the people did not make a show of resistance. The reply was that so long as they behaved themselves they would be treated with some consideration, but that where they showed fight there would be absolutely no mercy. That was the reason why such a large fraction of the population was taken unarmed and dealt with in the most inhuman way. So long as no resistance was offered only a percentage of the Christian population living under the rule of the Sultan had their throats cut. They had no choice; they were not allowed to emigrate from the country. An offer was made to transport them to some other part of Europe, but the Sultan could not afford to let them go, because these men had the best business brains of the whole country. They were, in a sense, the goose that laid the golden eggs. It was from them that a lot of the revenues of the Turkish empire were drawn, and so they were not allowed to go, and they were not allowed to leave the country to this day. So long as, in the modern phrase, they "took it lying down "they could quietly have their throats cut, but where they showed one particle of resistance there were such conse- quences as the father of a household being shut up with his family, straw and petroleum thrown into the house, and the whole family being burnt alive. The only protection they had was where a European was associated with them, because the Sultan knew that if a European was harmed, there would have to be some reparation—perhaps of a financial character. Therefore in some cases, masses of the population were saved by the missionaries who refused to leave their people when they took refuge in the churches. But in other cases where these unfortunate people fled to their churches,they were treated in exactly the same inhuman way, and as many as two or three thousand were burnt together in their churches. He was mentioning these facts to illustrate

TIIE EXTREME CYNICISM that had crept into the conduct of foreign affairs by the powers of Europe owing to the gospel of luck and force and crude imperialism which had unfortunately become much too prevalent in the last two decades. People said at once "What canyon do? England is powerless." England was nothing of the kind—applause)—neither were the other countries. They were coercing the Turkish empire every day of the week. They took care that the tobacco monopoly was collected, and that taxes which were ear-marked for the nations which had financed Turkey were paid to time. If they were not paid, or if any attack was made on a subject or a Consul belonging to any of those countries, pressure was brought to bear at once. Mr. Crosfield quoted an illus- tration of this, showing how, in the case of a Russian subject being killed, immediate action was taken. Yet, in large districts of Macedonia, villages were being burnt and people were being tortured, but the Russian Government never attempted to interfere. We ourselves could go on AN EXPEDITION INTO THIBET which nobody defended or pretended to defend now and which, if Russia had been at peace would have exasperated her to the last degree. She could not interfere because her hands were full. But it did not occur to us to make her difficulty an opportunity of seeing that the reforms on which we professed to insist should be carried out, so as to prevent the Turkish Government plundering, robbing, illtreatin-, and even , torturing the Christian races that lived wider them. When we remembered that the Macedonian people were suffering these extreme cruelties owing to our having 11 torn up the treaty of San Stefano, and, having under

any spirit recrimination. There were plenty of friends of theirs who thought differently to him about the war, and who thought petfectly honestly, but he was sure they would all let bve-gones be bye-gones as regarded that issue and join with the party in defence of the great cause of Free Trade. (Applause). It seemed to him, however, that knowing the opinion of the great body of the Liberal party they ought not to altogether forget what had happened in South Africa as it had an enormous effect on the position of things to-day. Mr. Crosfield proceeded to read the summary as follows :—The South African account is now familiar to every elector. He has got the facts and figures by heart. He knows all the TRICKS AND CONSPIRACIES OF THE MINEOWNERS from the Jameson Raid onwards by which this country was lured into war. He knows that while the war cost two hundred and fifty millions, that twenty thousand lives were sacrificed in it, that it increased the national debt by a hundred and fifty millions, reduced consols from £llO to £B5, the lowest point in our time, and that for every soldier we kept in South Africa six years ago to-day we keep five at an increased annual cost of nearly two millions sterling. And what have we got in return? We have got 30,000 Chinese slaves at a shilling a day: we have got a sham constitution which places the whole executive power and the whole of the taxa- tion of the country in the hands of the creatures of the Randlords, we have got a bad debt of thirty millions and we have a country seething with discontent and indignation. To-day it is seen what the war was waged for. It was waged to crush the Boer rule which had refused Chinese labour, to put the control of thecountry in the hands of tie mineowners, and to shut out the British workman, who, in the language of Mr. Lionel Phillips, the Tory candidate for Paddington, lean article the mineowners "cannot afford." Mr. Creswell has shown at the Village Main Reef that white labour was not only possible, but more profitable. But when he had proved it be found that he had proved too much for his directors. And to-day Mr. Cresswell is one of the group of honest Englishmen on the Rand who, having advocated the war, are now conscious of the appalling consequences, and are standing shoulder to shoulder with the Boers in the hope of saving the unhappy country from absolute disaster. For everyone realises to-day that it is not a question of "affording" white labour, but a question of "fearing" the white labourer which is at the root of the whole business. The case has been stated with excellent frankness by one of the few mineowners who have English names, Mr. Rudd, when he said: "Could we (the mineowners) replace 200,000 native workers by 100,000 unskilled whites they would simply hold the government in the hollow of their hands, and, without any disparagement of the British labourer, I prefer to see the more intellec- tual section of the community at the helm." And Mr. Lyttleton and Lord Milner have a similar preference. They have brought in the Chinese serf, they have ejected the white man, they have given those who remain a sham vote, and they have left the .f‘ intellectuals " of the type of Mr. Belt and Mr. Eckstein, Mr. Shumacher and Mr. Werner at the helm. In conclusion, Mr. Crosfield quoted John Burns' opinion that we had been witnessing a Jingo Rake's progress— Slavery, Protection, and lastly, what they regretted to see advocated by men of high position in England, con- scription. They would probably very soon be called upon to decide at all events one wide-spread, far-reach- ing issue. They would be called upon to RAISE TIM COST OF LIVING under the pretence that it would make them richer, and they would be called upon in doing so to push thousand more into that deplorable quagmire at the bottom of the social ladder. They did not hear much said about the fiscal policy now because the country had made up its mind, and we in Lancashire above all, who had such a vast industry at stake, were not going to be caught by chaff of that kind. The great politic 11 plunger of Birmingham appeared to have found out his mistake. He (Mr. Crosfield) had a personal interest in the question because his father and grandfather were privileged to be on very friendly terms for many years with John Bright and Richard Cobden—(applause)—who fought the battle of Free Trade. In Warrington he believed the cause of Free Trade and Liberalism had MADE A GREAT ADVANCE in the last twelve mouths, and he hoped that none of those present would ever forget the simple but beauti- ful words they listened to from the valliant and brilliant Welsh chieftain who visited them them the other day. Let them remember what he said : Freedom i 3 a good master. She pays well, she feeds well. Cobden and IBright struck the shackles from your trade. See that you walk freely throughout the world(Loud applause.) MR. VIVIAN AND PROTECTION. Mr. VIVIAN, in a powerful speech, said it was sugges- ted by some people that a Liberal could not be a patriot or an Imperialist. He thought the tone of their chair- man's remarks compared very favourably with the blatant stuff they got from too many platforms on the other side. (Hear, hear). If they could have brought before the electors a profit and loss account of the last nine or ten years of Tory Government, he did not think there could be any doubt as to what their verdict would be when they had the opportunity of expressing their opinion. (Applause ) The difficulty %YRS to make the profit and loss account clearer to the ordinary mind. Of late years we had increased our' democratic machinery, we had increased the pro- portion of life over which our representative Government held sway, far more than we had increased the power of the individual mind to take its share of the responsibility of the work of driving that representative Government. It was very important that Liberal and progressive people of all kinds should do something to try and stir up the political instincts of the British people so that they might be equal to their new powers and opportunities. They did not want the power to be used to supporta crude imperial- ism grinding out the fortunes of a limited few, but they , should endeavour to inspire the democratic machinery

BIR. HOWES AND TEIE COMING FIGHT. Mr. JosErn HOWES delivered a short speech, and said it was their endeavour to raise imperialism to a ' plane as high as it had ever reached in any part of the history )f the Borough. The campaign was to be an educational protest against tyranny and villainy in high places : and they felt there was sufficient moral fibre in the workingmen to respond to such an appeal as that. (Applause). With such a candidate, with such a cause, and such supporters, he thought they were going to win the fight. (Applause.) Mr. Howes concluded by moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Vivian. Mr. EDMUND OSBORNE seconded, and said Mr. Vivian's scldress should inspire even the most progres- sive of them to do something in the fight which they expected almost any day. As a Progressive he welcomed the lucid exposition of the questions which the speaker had dealt with, and he was satisfied that if the democracy could have those views placed before them as clearly as they had been that night, there would be considerably less belief in Tory magnanimity. Workingmen had been gulled to a very great extent by those employers who looked upon men not as human beings, but more or less as tools, as part and parcel of the machinery. Times however, were changing, and the workers were now beginning to take an sctive interest in politics, and the Government would have to grant them equal rights. "We shall look" he said, in conclusion, to the Liberal Govern- ment, which I hope will soon be in power, to do some- thing to place workingmen on a higher level than they are at the present time." (Applause). In putting the motion to the meeting, the CHAIRMAN emphasised the value of propagandist work in a place like Warrington which had far too long been dominated by Tory influences. Those who were so concerned in the great controversy they were engaged in, looked very greatly indeed to the efforts and the influence of the Progressive Labour League, of which Mr. Osborne was the hon. treasurer, in order that the' views which had been so splendidly put before them by Mr. Vivian should be well circulated and driven home in the town. (Applause.) The vote was heartily agreed to. THE BOROUGH MEMBER'S POSITION. A vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman on the proposition of Mr. VivrAs. In responding, Mr. CROSFIELD said it was a signifi- cant point that their own distinguished member for Warrington had given Protection a very wide berth of late. It was not so long since he was cock-a-whoop " about this fantastic policy, and the great high priest of it all, Colonel Sir Howard Vincent was telling him (Mr. Crosfield) that he was coming "to Warrington to smash, demolish and pulverise the Free I raclers. (Laughter.) It was not a little significant that the tune had changed, but they knew what was in the wind and what they had to fight against, Mr. Vivian's state- ment of what the Protective forces were and of what they meant in their present as well as their more remote effect, was a reminder which he (the chairman) was sure none of them would forget. (Applause).

(Applause). _ _ THIS FRAUDULENT BILL . . - .

occupied to-day. Mr. Chamberlain was concerned about the opinion of the working classes on this subject. There was no demand for this bill from them. The bill was supported on one genuine and one fictitious basis. The genuine basis was that certain people who were deseased or who were criminals came into this country every year. Everybody admitted that in that respect there might be a legitimate demand for legislation." There was already, said Mr. Crosfield, a medical examination to prevent diseased aliens coming into this country and what was required was that the examination should be more comprehensive Mr. Kier Hardy continued" but this bill was spoken of in the House, in the press, and on the platform of hon. gentlemen opposite not as a bill to keep out criminals and diseased aliens, but as a bill to keep out workmen who came here to compete with native labour, in that sense it was f raudulent, deceitful and dish9nourable. We did not want diseased people, and we did not want criminals coming into England, but the proportion of I poor people who!came to this country and were a burden on the rates was so trifling, that they could under- stand why a man like Mr. Asquith declined to treat the Bill as of first-class importance. His (Mr. Crosfleld's) informant, and he was a gentleman who was very reliable, said that £28,000 per annum was the total charge upon this country with all its vast riches, and at a time like the present, when Russia was going through her last agony, and when so many wretched people were fleeing from that autocratic and cruel Government, it did seem a little hard that we should shut our doors to the few POLITICAL REFUGEES who found their way here. (Applause.) So much• for the alien question. He hoped they would keep their heads cool and reserve their judgment upon any other side issue which might be brought before them. He would have the pleasure of being present at one or two meetings next week when he would have something to say,upon the positive policy for which they had to fight. I The Liberal Party were not going to fight the battle of Free Trade purely as a negative policy. They had an enormous amount of work to do which every true progressive must fight for, but even if they were to fight a negative battle it would be good enough to fight against the re-actionary principle which had introduced slavery into the BritishEmpire—(applause)-- and which Was trying to introduce Protection, and the dreadful policy of conscription. (Applause.) They had, however, a great deal more to fight for. The "Observer" he noticed had been chaffing him about being a poor speaker. He did not mind the "Observer's" chaff and had never set up as being an orator, but be had been brought up in Liberal principles and he could say that during he so that he had taken a keen an activeinterest n politics he had been convinced that Mr. John Morley n he k said broadmindedthat the ' t 2 0 years o r yd lay than owhnee in Liberal body. (Applause.) It was a matter upon which he felt very strongly and although they had powerful advancementne v e r s a i d ot fr truer humanity thing ltah influences against them in Warrington if they would only do their part, and make the Progressive Labour League the greatest factor in the town for progression, he would to the best of his ability do his. (Applause.) MR. VIVIAN'S SPEECH. Mr. VIVIAN asked those present to look at the Aliens question in a broad-minded way so that they might not take a serious re-actionary step in connection with political life. If there was one country more than another which owed something to freedom and free admission of the whole of the people in the world it was this country. Our greatest industries had their origin in the fact that England even in the bad past had the good Sense to recognize the importance of freedom in the interchange of human beings between other countries and our own. (Applause.) There were to-day more Englishmen in France than :here were Frenchmen in England. The same Lthing l applied to Germany. By excluding the Alien instead of helping British workingmen we would be STRIKING A BLOW AT OUR. GREAT INDUSTRIES. by creating a bad feeling between ourselves and those countries from which we as a commercial nation derived great profit and a great number of blessings. If their political opponents wanted to begin clearing out the alien they might begin in Park-lane. (Applause.) If they cleared Park-lane from one end to the other and put those aliens into the Channel, England would be millions of pounds better off. It was those men who came here with un-English names, who got into Parlia- ment, who influenced the Press and who were able to pool up their millions whom he would like to see kicked out of the country. It was the men who had built mansions in Park-lane out of the money they had taken from the workingman and who had organized to promote their own interests and advantage who were fleecing us. Did any artisan in Warrington, 4id he (the speaker) as a workman fear the com- petition of the puny, half-starved creatures fleeing from the tyranny in Russia ? It was ridiculous to suppose that they did. His blood did not boil at the fact that those creatures came to get a few years happi- ness out of their life, but his blood did boil at the robbery by the alien in Park-lane. (Applause.) Mr. Vivian proceeded to deal briefly but vigorously with the Fiscal question. Continuing, he said, they were Free Traders and as such he would go forward and demand a re-adjustment of the land laws—(applause)— and see that where land had increased in value as the result of industry,that that land contributed something to the burden Of the rates of the town. Mr. CTOSBeId was an enthusiastic supporter of the re-arrangement of the whole basis of taxation so that instead of idleness deriving a living from industry idleness should be taxed. Better conditions were necessary for the lives of those who worked in the factories and that could be brought about by A BETTER SYSTEM OF TAXATION. He never knew a political fight with graver issues than the one they had before them, issues each one of which was vital to the welfare of our country. There was the question of education, and they had to see that the education of their children was something more than a

struggle of theologians who were desirous of advancing their particular views. Government departments had to be re-organized, and the condition of the working classes had to be improved. The responsibility for this work rested with the voters individually, and it was for them to see that the reign of Toryism in Warrington was ended at the next election. (Applause). Mr. BARNES proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Vivian for his address. We had reason to complain of the want of attention displayed by Mr. Robert Pierpoint, who seemed to take his political duties in a happy-go- lucky sort of style. (Hear, hear). Councillor EVANS seconded in a brief but effective speech, and the vote was heartily accorded. Mr. VtvLis, in responding, moved a vote of thanks to Mr. A. H. Crosfield. The vote was heartily carried and a brig response by Mr. CROSFIELD brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: MEETING IN ST. BARNABAS' SCHOOL. -- Mr. Pierpoint Criticised.
div.p: MEETING IN ST. BARNABAS' SCHOOL. -- Mr. Pierpoint Criticised.

There was a large and enthusiastic gathering in the St. Harnabas' School, on Thursday, at a meeting which was held under the auspices of the League. The large room was crowded and a very hearty reception was accorded Mr. Crosfield as he entered Mr. Crosfield occupied the chair, being supported by Mr. H. Vivian, Councillor J. Wilkinson, and Messrs. J. Howes, C. E. Parker, W. Furness, C. Jackson Holmes, J. A. J. Morton and T. Barnes. MR. CROSFIELD REPLIES TO MR. PIERPOINT.

div.head: ALIENS QUESTION.
div.p: THE ALIENS QUESTION.

Mr. CROSFIELD said we did not know when we were going to fight the great battle which ley before us. It might be next month, it might be next autumn and some of those who were supposed to be what was called "in the know " had said we might have to wait until a year next autumn. Personally he did not believe we would have to wait until a year next autumn, but whether the fight came next month or next autumn. Mr. Balfour was going to ask the country to decide upon his policy. The extraordinary thing was that probably not a single individual in his constituency—West Manchester—knew what Mr. Balfour's policy was (Applause) We in Warrington were certainly luckier in one respect because OUR PRESENT MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT

had got down on one side of the fence and was what is popularly known as a " wholehogger," and he, for one, was very glad that there could therefore be no misunderstanding on that point. (Applause.) We I had seen the most weighty, well informed and influential men on the side of the Conservative party refusing to have anything to do with this now " fangled " idea of upsetting the whole of the fiscal and commercial policy of this country. (Applause.) To them honour lot it be said they repudiated anything of the kind. Men who were a few years ago the laughing stock of the country I—men like Sir Howard Vincent and Mr. Chaplin—were now forsooth the leaders in whose wake their good ' friend Mr. Pierpoint was bent on following. (Applause.) As late as last March Mr. Pierpoint had been giving us the pure milk of Protection and he (the speaker) repeated that he was glad that we in Warrington at any rate I would not have to grope in the mists of illusions of those who professed what was called the Balforian theory. Mr. Pierpoint had certainly nailed his colours to the mast—pluckily if they would—but he was afraid , Mr. Pierpoint had jumped at THE FALLACIOUS CONCLUSIONS OF TLIE PROTECTIONIST and in jumping at them he had landed with both feet. (Applause.) Ho thought he might give a quotation

div.head: ST. JOHN'S WARD SOCIAL.
div.p: ST. JOHN'S WARD SOCIAL.

The members of the St. John's Ward Liberal Committee spent a very enjoyable evening on Monday, when they held a social evening in the Brick-street Chapel. An excellent tea was served, at which a fair number sat down, the tables being presided over by Mesdames Furness, Magiun, Vose' Bailey, Fysh and m S'w, and the Misses Flinston. NIG W. Furness pre- sided over the subsequent proceedings, being supported by Councillor Maginn, Messrs. Joseph Howes, C Jackson Holmes, J. \rose, Plinston and Fysh. Mr. FURNESS emphasised the value of social functions in political life, as bringing the members of a party more into touch with each other. (Hear, heir.) He hoped the influence of the social gatherings which were being held in connection with the Liberal party, would have be lasting and would tend to unite the party and make it the power which it ought to be in the town. So far as the prospects of winning an election went he thought they in St. John's Ward were well able to do their share. (Applause.) In u sense he thought it was the most important ward in the town on account of the number of voters and because they had a large section of the younger element amongst them. Mr. Furness impressed upon his hearers the great need for securing the interest of the younger generation and bring them in line with the rest of the ward. He was sorry they had not Mr. Cros- field with them, but his absence was unavoidable. How- ever, they hoped he would be amongst them in the near future. (Applause.) _ _

11 Councillor ALIGINN said he was glad of the oppor- tunity to speak for Liberalism, liberty and common sense. (Hear, hear.) The reason ho was a Liberal was because theirs was the only platform which gave the true hearing to the workers of the country. Ho was a Liberal when he was poorer than the poorest man in that room, and he was a Liberal now for the same reason, and recent records of the present Government had served to make him all the more convinced in his opinion. (Applause.) The present administration had increased the expenditure enormously, while in the war they started in South Africa they made our country ridiculous in the eyes of the world. When they were returned to Parliament again to finish the war muddle they passed the Education Act despite the great opposi- tion to it. There were many who thought the Act was a benefit to Catholics, but it was not so. Catholics had built schools for their children at a great sacrifice and in many cases the mortgages were not paid off with the result that they had still to pay that, in addition to the heavy education rates. Tbe working classes were not getting their money's worth out of the Education Act. In fact, the Act was passed first for the purpose of gaining votes and to shift respon- sibilities from the rich and put it on the shoulders of the poor. (Hear, hear), The conservatives had striven in many directions to propose something which would gain them some favour, and as they had failed they were falling back on Home Rule. It was not necessary to tell Liberals that that Home Rule cry was a war cry only, but it was necessary to impress it upon others. It was acknowledged that the Liberals would get into power at the next election and it was their duty to see that Warrington had a Liberal as its representative. (Applause). Mr. HOWES regretted the absence of Mr. Crosfleld. The prospective Liberal candidate was, he said, estab- lishing another great industry, and it had necessitated an immense amount of work. He had been engaged on it night and day, but now it was fairly established, and before long he believed that industry—one entirely anart from soap—would spread itself all through England. (Applause.) Mr. Crosfleld, however, would be with them on many occasions during the next few weeks, when they would deal with the new stand taken up by the leaders of the Conserva- tive Party, who seemed to have decided to forget all about the " falling empire." The Home Rule ques- tion was again being introduced. He was sorry English people did not thoroughly understand the Irish question. If they only did, Home Rule would no longer be the bogey it was with certain classes. The latest piece of Government " heroism" was to have a British gunboat to assist the landlords to get their rent, turning out blue jackets into bailiffs. It was despicable. (Applause.) He hoped at the next election the people would emanci- pate Warrington. " You have just won the cup," he sail in conclusion "the next thing is to turn out the Tory candidate and put in a Liberal. (Applause.) Do your part,and we shall take our stand with the reformers of the country." (Applause.) During the evening musical items were given by the Apollo Quartet party who were heartily encored for their selections, and Miss L. Plinston, who was also re- called, Mr. Cook was highly successful with a humorous recitation.
Votes of thanks to the Chairman,artistes and the ladies who had assisted at tea, concluded the meeting.

div.head: WARRINGTON GROCERS' ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON GROCERS' ASSOCIATION.
Annual Meeting.

The members of the Warrington and District Grocers' and Provision Dealers' Association held their fourth annual meeting at the British Workman Cocoa Rooms on Wednesday evening. Mr. J. Gandy presided over a small attendance.

div.head: ANNUAL REPORT.
div.p: ANNUAL REPORT.

The SECRETARY (Mr. J. P. Gorst) presented a satis- factory annual report in which he stated that the com- mittee had again to record a year of solid beneficent work. The past year, owing to the pressure of Imperial and municipal burdens, coupled with an unexampled period of stagnation in trade, had been an I especially trying one for members of the trade. The ' committee were, however, hopeful that the worst was over, and that they might look forward to the future with a brighter hope. There were still many elements of disquietude in the commercial world, and the com- mittee would urge upon their members the necessity of consolidating their position whenever an opportunity of doing, so presented itself. The committee had made enquiries and had been anxious to appoint a consulting analyst to the Association, but their efforts to find a local man were unsuccessful. Further action would probably be taken in the matter, which became increasingly vital to the members. The committee were anxious to become affiliated with the Chamber of Commerce but correspondence up to the , present had not brought about a satisfactory arrange- ment, as the terms did not commend themselves to the committee. The attention of the Warrington repro- ' sentative in the House of Commons had been drawn to the Sale of Better Bill and he had been requested to further the same and also to uphold the standard of 16 per cent, of water. A favourable reply had been received, but the supineness of the Government and the general apathy of .a rapidly-expiring Parliament did not tend to filreier the prospects of this invaluable measure. Refer- ence was made to the death of IVlr.Edwin Richardson,an honorary member of the Association since its formation, and of Mr. Henry Milling who, though not a member of the Association, had on several occasions borne testimony to their good work. The report was unanimously adopted. On the motion of Mr. KAY seconded by Mr. RICHARD- SON, Mr. Gandy was heartily thanked for his services during the past year as president of the Association. Mr. GANDY, in returning thanks, said he was very anxious to see the members of the Association working , amicably together and hoped that the good feeling which had shown itself in the past would continue. The officers of the Association were also heartily thanked for their past services.
ri.ECTION OF.OFFICERS.

Mr. GANDY expressed a desire that the meeting should appoint a younger man as president of the Association. hut the members present declined to accept his sugges- tion and unanimously re-elected him to that office. The secretary and treasurer, Mr. J. P. Gorst, and Mr. W. Povey were re-appointed as were also the solicitor to the Association (Mr. .T. S. Steel) and the auditor (Mr. Bowdon). The retiring members of the committee (Messrs. Gerrard, Isaac, Bowdon, Reading, Owen, W. Taylor and Stringer) were re-elected, and the vice- presidents, Messrs. Kay, Richardson and Monks were also re-appointed. Mr. PovEy stated that the Association had a balance in hand of .£ll Bs. The question of the appointment of a consulting analyst was left in the hands of the committee.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

Warrington are to be congratulated upon a very promising start in league cricket. The conditions for the opening match under South West Lancashire League auspices on Saturday were well nigh ideal, and there was quite an encouraging attendance at Arpley where Stanley were accounted for in no half-hearted style. There should be a brighter era in store for the Warring- ton club now that the much-talked-of league is an accomplished fact. Judging from their performance on Saturday our local wielders of the willow intend to make a bold bid for honours,and enthusiasts are already inspired with hopes that Warrington will earn a name for itself in the cricket world.

The Stanley eleven made a surprisingly poor show. They ed their opponents to run up the respectable total of 184, and could only respond with 57. Several of the Warrington batsmen were in fine form, and gave the visiting bowlers and fielders a livelier time than they bargained for. W. Richardson, a young player who rendered good service last season, gave a splendid exibi- tion. He hit out with refreshing vigour, and on five occasions dispatched the ball to the boundary. When bowled by Sharp he had placed 41 to his credit—an achievesient which deserves the warmest praise.

The Warrington captain, E. A. Connor, once more proved his capabilities ci a scorer, and ran up 38, his hits including five fours. It was a coincidence that Alf. Thewlis, the ex-prefessional,and Percy Mason the club's new professional, each made 23. J. Thompson was re- sponsible for 19, ancl;Ml. H. Podmore knocked up 12.

The Stanley contingent gave a very tame batting display. The scoring was practically left to one player, S. G. Moore, who made 32 out of the 57 for which the innings closed. None of the other visitors attained double figures.

Warrington have secured a very capable professional in Percy Mason and he acquitted himself decidedly well on Saturday. As before mentioned, his innings realized 23, and in addition he bowled with disastrous effect to the visitors, capturing seven wickets at the ridiculously small cost of 30 runs. E. A. Connor took two wickets for 7 runs.
To-day (Saturday) Warrington 'decide another league match at home, and hope to triumph over the Prescot eleven.

Warrington second also came out of their first league encounter with flying colours. Stanley should retain rather unpleasant recollections of their part in th. fixture, for they had to admit defeat to the extent of 124. Going to the wicket first the Liverpool men were all dismissed for 44, the batsmen being quite unable to make headway against the deliveries of 1). Plinston and W. Bennett. To Warrington's grand total of 168, E. Pierpoint contributed an excellent 47, while A. Duck- worth and A. Plinston each coupled 32.
Newton and St. Helens were the only other league clubs to try conclusions on Saturday and Newton NN er e victorious in both first and second division matches.

Most of the junior teams commenced operations on Saturday, and some capital games were witnessed. Sankey Wire Mills administered an uncommonly severe drubbing to Knotty Ash who gave a wretched account of themselves. Their combined efforts produced only 10 runs, and the Wire Mills were able to pile on a majority of 90. Burton and Gleave wrought great havoc with the ball, the first named capturing six wickets for 8 runs, and Gleave four for 7. Brough, N. Cook, Walsh, Hawthorn, and F. Taylor distinguished themselves in the batting department.

Latchford Baptists visited Penketh and suffered defeat by a margin of 37. Tho victors had a good bats- man in Ward who knocked up 21. Latchford Baptist 2nd were more fortunate, the match with Widnes St. Mary's ending in their favour by the narrow majority of 3. Callon (16) was the top scorer.

St. James's scored a victory at the expense of the Secondary School. The best innings was that of C. Massie who ran up 22 for the winners. Grappenhall St. Wilfred's had the best of the match with Widnes White Rose and Moore and Daresbury triumphed over Alvanley.

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

The fine weather last Saturda—y proved a great incen- tive to bowlers to indulge in their favourite sport, and consequently local greens were largely patronized. The Works Association and the League are in full swing and Saturday witnessed in connection each organiza- tion two of the finest struggles over seen on local greens. To-day should also produce a splendid fight in connection with the Works Association. Both com- petitors give promise of an usually successful season.

Mr. England has been acquainted with the decision of the Warrington League with regard to his gift of for a Warrington Championship prize. He holds with the view I expressed several weeks ago, that the com- petition should not be confined to the League but should be open to two representatives from each club in the town—the players to be selected by the clubs with which they are connected:lf the original decision of the League were to be carried out, the winner of the main could hardly be styled the champion of the town -but would merely be entitled to the honour of the champion- ship of the League. I agree with Mr. England that if all the clubs in Warrington are represented the competi- tion would create a great interest in the town and wouldhelp on good sport. There is no doubt that his suggestion will be acted upon and under the control of the League Committee the main should prove an un- usually successful and attractive one.

A sub-committee of the To xn Hall, Park and Baths Comnritee has been appointed to consider the question of opening the Corporatian green in Victoria Park, and the purchase of bowls, Scc. The matter will be con- sidered immediately, and the green will probably be open to players during 'the course of the next few weeks.

WORKS COMPETITION. Pearson and Knowles (No. 1.) team, last season's champions, were in a record-breaking humour on Satur- day, and their aptituderfor scoring caused a great shock to their opponents. Naylor's are not by any .means a strong combination and naturally they viewed the en- counter with some alarm;but certainly they'expected to give a much better account of themselves than actually proved to be the case. By winning every game and the match by a majority of 101, the Pearson and Knowles team have established a record which will doubtless stand good for some time—in fact it is improbable that it will ever be beaten. Naylor's took their defeat ex- tremely well and returned a cheerful negative to repeated enquiries as to whether they were down- hearted.

The start was not one to inspire them with confid- ence as with two men off the green they were in arrears to the extent of 26 points. Matters did not improve as the defeat of E. Chorley placed them to a greater dis- advantage. It at first appeared as though Chorley was to record the first victory for Naylor's as after the fifth end he lead by 4-1. Hardman however, rose to the occasion and by a single and a double drew level. From this point he never looked back and gradually increased his lead to one of 15-3. P. Ball proved a much better trundler than J. Jenks and led from the start. A sterner struggle was witnessed between J. Howarth and H. Higham. At the eighth end Naylor's man took the lead but two ends later Higham drew level and by two doubles and two singles further impi oved his position. Howarth made a brave effort and for a time was the principal one to trouble the scorers. His hopes ran high when he reached 13-14, but the next end proved his undoing and Higham recorded a fifth win for Pearson and Knowles. From this point the issue of the'match was not in doubt, the next three members of the defeated team never drawing level with their opponents. J. Potter made an effort to stem the tide of disaster and ran J. Gibbons close until the score stood G. He then, however, fell off and Gibbons reached his points, while Naylor's man added two chalks to his score. Some amusement was caused by the game between J. Block and W. Mee, in which the only question was as to the rate at which Mee could reach his points. He opened the game with a couple of singles and ran out winner in eight more ends, Block not being allowed to score a single point. R. Wicks strove hard to prevent the winners achieving a record, and at one time it appeared as though he would succeed. Obtaining a lead of 7-4, he went from this to 9-5, when, however, massey com- menced to make his presence felt, and drew level at 11. The next two ends were divided, and then Massey secured a double. A single to each player left the victory to Pearson and Knowles by 15-13.

The two fixtures in connection with the competition afforded a striking contrast the game between the Firth and Longford teams being an unusually keen struggle, the result being in doubt until the last two playefs were left on the green. Longford made a good start, the first game going in their favour by ten points. By defeatiltg J. Clare, F. Rathbone reduced their lead by eight points and the next game gave the Firth team ithe advantage. T. Clare and H. Atherton early on ran I each other very close, and peeled successively at 4,5, 6 I and 7. Atherton then took the lead, which he kept until the end,!when the balance was reversed and stood at 2in favour of the Longford players. W. Simister further improved the position of his team, givin his opponent little chance, and winning bi 11-15. Lomas played well until the eighth end, when he drew level, but from that point he was in arrears.
At this point the interest of the spectators was fully aroused, and the efforts of the players

were repeatedly cheered. The interest was increaed by the next game going to the Firth men, and the scores with six men off the green stood at 70-75. The hopes of the Firth players ran high but unfortunately for them J. Daintith was not strong enough for Sudlow, and as those two players left the green eight points separated the teams. Stringer occasioned the leaders some uneasiness but lost to W. Holloway by one point. At the fifteenth end he led by two points but Holloway tied with a double. By alter- nate chalks the players kept level until the score was 14 all when Holloway placed a splendid wood and won by the odd point. The position was not improved, from 'the point of view of the Firth team, as the result of the next game J. Wilcocks losing to J. Simister by 14-15.

The succession of victories had inspired the Longfora men with confidence of ultimate success, but their assurance received an immediate shock. Playing against Ashton, C. Holloway never appeared to be quite happy and only got into the run of the game when it was too late, 'e heing defeated by 5 points. Atherton however retrieved the situation by running away from Quarry eleven points in favour of Longford separating the two teams when he left the green. T.Bolton, who is a fairly. prominent League player,was the hope of the Firth team but the task proved beyond his trength and Longford by seven points, won one of the hardest fought games ever witnessed in contmction with the competition.

The adjourned draw for the first round was made on Monday and resulted as follows :—Corporation v. Greenings ; Houghton's v. London and North \Vestern Walkers Brewery v. Thewlis and Griffiths ; Cheshire Lines Committee v. Orford Tannery: P. and K. (No. 3) v. Riehmonds ; St. Helens Cable v. Rylands Netting ;- Whitecross (2) v. Castle Rubber; Fletchers v. Forshavn Crosfiehis v. Rylands (No. 1) ; Howley Tannery V. Pearson and Knowles (No. 2). Stubb's were given a• bye.

The matches will be resumed to-day (Saturday) when, two games will be decided. Interest will be chiefly in the encounter between London and North Western and Houghton's as the teams aie very evenly matched. Last year the two teams met and the railway men carried off the victory. To-day Houghton's mean to have their revenge, and as they are a considerably improved combination they will probably succeed. They must not however, ;- take things too much for granted as the London and North-Western players can when necessary rise to the ~. occasion • and it would net surprise me to see them repeat last year's performance. The players in the other ~ two teams are little known and it is not expected that either combination will prove strong enough to progress far through the intermediate rounds. With such teams it is hard to foretell the victors and therefore I will abstain from any prophecies.

WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE. The Fearnhead players had a rather busy time on Saturday and as the result of the two matches which they played at borne. they annexed four points in the league table. In each case they fully expected to, and did win, but in the game with the Bull's Head team they had a pretty bad fright before they achieved the victory. The men from Church-street went to Fearn- head determined to give a good account of themselves. and they succeeded. With four men off the green they led by 17 points and matters for them looked particu- larly rosy. The next few games produced little change and the Ball's Head players were rejoicing over a prospective victory when the defeat of E. Shaw and C. Ball made the scores more level. By defeating R. Fairbrother 15-13 James Andrews further decreased the lead and with two men on the green four points separated the teams. To say that the final stages of the game aroused enthusiasm is to put it mildly, especially when it was seen that Swanton of the Bull's Head team was being beaten. Swanton made a great effort which however proved unavailing, James Roberts almost wiping off the Fearnhead arrears. With W. Andrews and A. Cleave on the green, no one knew exactly what was going to happen. Cleave is a young bowler who last year made some surprisingly good wins, while Andrews, ~; on the other hand, is a trundler of no i ' particular brilliance, though steady. Gleave's inexperience proved fatal, and the Bull's Head players had the mortification of seeing their lead reversed and Fearnhead carry off the victory by five points. From the match it is evident that there is to be a severe struggle for the championship, as last year the Bull's Head team lost the game at Fearnhead by 38 points. It is apparent that their play has greatly improved, and if Saturday's form is maintained, some of the stronger combinations in the League are going to receive a pretti severe shock.

The other team which fell a victim to Fearnhead vras the Cemetery, which lost by 19 points. The match did not arouse any particular display of enthusiasm, 05 throughout Fearnhead had the balance of points in their favour.
To-day (Saturday) the first of the series of mains 5.11 connection with the League will he held on the Cemetery green. A large number of entries have been received and a close fight should result.

-- Penketh Park gave a poor account of themselves on the Sankey Chapel House green on Ssturday, being de- feated by SO points, only one man on their team, A. Bowyer, succeeded in winning his game and of the remainder only four reached double figures. They will have to considerably improve their play or they will be strong candidates for the wooden spoon at the close of the season. Sankey on the other hand, are in tip toP form and should occupy a high position in the league table. They have a chance for the championship but before they carry off the laurels they will have to meet the Bulls Head and Cemetery teams.two of the strongest combinations in the town, and these matches will pro- bably prove their undoing.

OTHER MATCHES. The Warrington men started we', and obtained a useful lead. Unfortunately a success/0" of defeats placed them in a disadvantageous position, and the final rally came too late, Stonkport qualifYlegl for the second round of the competition with a majori- of 30 points.

--- RELIGIOUS INSTRUCTION IN CHESHIRE SCHOOLS. Interesting Scheme. The Cheshire Education Committee have approved a scheme of religions instruction formulated by a special Committee, of which Colonel Dixon, chairman of the County Council, was chairman, for use in the provided schools of the county. The report recommending the scheme stated :—" The committee are most anxious that neither the teachers nor the children should look upon the religious instruction as a harden. • In the committee's opinion this portion of the work of education, whilst of the highest import- ance, is of special difficulty, demanding the utmost skill, discretion, and sympathy on the part of the teacher. The chief object to be kept in view is to develop the spiritual faculties, and so to inculcate the highest standard of morality. The follow- ing suggestion to teachers do not refer specially to the time devoted to religious instruction but are intended to apply to the whole tone and teaching of the school: (1) Duties to parents and to our country to be often explained; (2) temperance, purity, and general self- restraint,in daily life to be taught; (3) children to be warned against evils arising from drinking, gambling, juvenile smoking, and worthless literature; (4) courtesy to be inculcated by action and teach- ing; (5) kindness to animals to be taught; (9 thrift to be encouraged; (7) healthy exer- cise and sports to be encouraged, but not to such an extent as to interfere with work and duty. In every school the period for religious observances and. Instruction shall be in the morning, for not less than thirty minutes daily from the opening of the school. The morning session shall be opened and the afternoon session closed by the use of one of the hymns and prayers approved by the committee. Tht religious in- struction shall be given by the responsible teachers on the staffs of the schools, provided that no teacher be called upon to give religious instruction who has con- scientious objections to so doing, and makes a state- ment to that effect to the managers." —ee— • It is (evident that the popularity of Henry Seton Merriman did not die with him. His great story "The Sowers" has emerged triumphantly from the test of the sixpenny reprint, in which form it seems destined to establish a record for sales. Messrs. Newnes, by arrangement with Messrs. Smith, Elder and Co., are about to issue the whole of Merriman's novels in their Sixpenny Series, and have commissioned the well- known artist Mr. A. S. Hartrick to illustrate all the stories. "In Kedar's Tents" is almost ready, and the other novels will follow at monthly intervals.

Diagram 99 shows several half-ball right- angle screws. Owing to the cue ball being in each case some distance away from the object there need be no fear of overscrewitr, the stroke even if it be played pretty hard (pro 7 vided that the object ball be, not taken fuller than half-ball), for owing to the friction: of the cloth the cue ball loses a considerable amount of its reverse rotation before it reaches the object ball. In fact, the ordinary player will find these half-ball right-angle screws easiest if played with plenty of strength. A good player would, however, generally play the screws shown on Diagram 97 comparatively slowly, and would take the object ball a shade fuller than half-ball. Of course, played in this way such strokes are somewhat .more difficult, but the compensation lies in better control of the object ball. Of the strokes shown on Diagram 99 the cannon is the easiest, simply because there is always more margin for direction when playing a cannon than when playing an in-off.
